methods.name: PPO
methods.shipped_by: trl, `trl.experimental.ppo.PPOTrainer` / `PPOConfig` — not exported from the top-level `trl` package (confirmed by grepping `trl/__init__.py` at commit `2396dfe5d2be7b18c0b615d80957d64ecdeb7cc0`, which lists `GRPOConfig`/`GRPOTrainer` but no `PPOConfig`/`PPOTrainer`; the experimental subpackage's own `__init__.py` exports `PPOConfig` and `PPOTrainer` under `trl.experimental.ppo`) — an experimental, not top-level-supported, entry point. verl, `python3 -m verl.trainer.main_ppo` with `algorithm.adv_estimator: gae` — verl's own default advantage estimator, i.e
methods.variant_of: TRPO
methods.data_it_needs: prompts (or environment states) plus a way to score each generated rollout with a scalar reward — a reward model in the RLHF setting or an environment reward signal in the original paper's control-task experiments
methods.extra_models: always a value network (critic) — the objective's `L^VF` term is a per-timestep squared-error loss against a value target, combined with the clipped policy loss and an entropy bonus in `L^CLIP+VF+S` (Eq. 9); this is a full second network trained end-to-end, not optional in the paper's own definition
methods.when_to_pick: online RL when you can afford to train a full second network (the critic) alongside the policy and want a per-token learned baseline rather than a group- or batch-level one; the clipped or KL-penalized surrogate lets you take multiple SGD epochs per batch of on-policy data without the complexity of TRPO's constrained solve

methods.name: LORA
methods.full_name: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
methods.shipped_by: Hugging Face PEFT, whose top-level package exports `LoraConfig` and `get_peft_model` as the entry point, is the reference implementation and is under active development as HF's core parameter-efficient fine-tuning library
methods.variant_of: standard (full) fine-tuning, contrasted with adapter tuning
methods.data_it_needs: whatever the wrapped objective needs - LoRA supplies no data format of its own
methods.extra_models: none required by LoRA's own definition - it adds only the two low-rank matrices $A$, $B$ per targeted layer, and needs no value network, reference model, reward model, or judge
methods.when_to_pick: pick LoRA whenever full fine-tuning's memory or storage cost is the blocker and the task can tolerate a bounded, low-rank weight update - it is orthogonal to the training objective, so it composes with SFT, DPO, or an RL loop such as PPO or GRPO rather than competing with them

methods.name: DPO
methods.shipped_by: trl (`DPOTrainer`). verl ships no standalone DPO trainer or config recipe: its documented algorithms list (PPO, GRPO, DAPO, SPIN, SPPO, GPG, and related online recipes) does not include one. verl's own docs instead carry a design-pattern tutorial, "Extend to other RL(HF) algorithms," that walks through building an on-policy "Online DPO" on top of verl's actor/rollout infrastructure with placeholder pseudocode (a `generate_sequences` sampler, a `ReferencePolicy` worker, and a `DPOActor.update` with `self.loss_fn = xxx` left unfilled) — it is a walkthrough, not a runnable recipe
methods.variant_of: the PPO-based RLHF pipeline of Ziegler et al., of which DPO is a reparameterization that removes the explicit reward model and the RL optimizer
methods.data_it_needs: a static dataset of `(prompt, chosen, rejected)` triples — trl's `DPOTrainer` accepts this as `{"prompt":..., "chosen":..., "rejected":...}` in standard format or the equivalent conversational format with role/content lists
methods.extra_models: one frozen reference model, a copy of the policy at the start of training, used only for forward passes to compute the log-ratio in the loss (Eq. 7)
methods.when_to_pick: pick DPO when you already have (or can cheaply construct) a static dataset of paired preferences and do not want to run generation inside the training loop

methods.name: GRPO
methods.shipped_by: trl (`GRPOTrainer`), verl (`algorithm.adv_estimator: grpo`)
methods.variant_of: PPO
methods.data_it_needs: prompts from the distribution you care about (the paper's RL stage used around 144K chain-of-thought questions related to GSM8K and MATH from the SFT data), plus a reward source
methods.extra_models: never a value network
methods.when_to_pick: online RL when every sampled completion can be scored with a scalar reward (a programmable function or a reward model) and memory is tight - the group baseline replaces PPO's value network

methods.name: QLORA
methods.shipped_by: `transformers` `BitsAndBytesConfig` (`load_in_4bit`, `bnb_4bit_quant_type`, `bnb_4bit_use_double_quant`, `bnb_4bit_compute_dtype`) provides the quantization side, `peft` exports `LoraConfig`, `get_peft_model`, and `prepare_model_for_kbit_training` from its top-level package for the adapter side, and `trl`'s `SFTTrainer` accepts both a `quantization_config` and a `peft_config` together to run QLoRA-style supervised fine-tuning in one call
methods.variant_of: LoRA
methods.data_it_needs: whatever the outer training objective needs - QLoRA is a fine-tuning mechanism, not an objective
methods.extra_models: none beyond the base model itself
methods.when_to_pick: pick QLoRA over plain LoRA when the base model itself does not fit in available GPU memory at 16-bit - QLoRA's own comparison shows 4-bit NF4 with double quantization matching 16-bit LoRA's MMLU accuracy at every LLaMA size from 7B to 65B (Table 4, mean 53.1 vs 53.0), so the quantization costs no accuracy at the scales tested

methods.name: DAPO
methods.shipped_by: trl (`GRPOTrainer`/`GRPOConfig`, with `loss_type="dapo"` as the default loss and `epsilon_high`/`mask_truncated_completions` as opt-in flags on the same trainer - there is no separate `DAPOTrainer`); verl (`recipe/dapo`, a documented reproducible recipe of scripts and config on top of verl's PPO/GRPO Ray trainer, launched via `run_dapo_qwen2.5_32b.sh`, not a standalone top-level trainer class)
methods.variant_of: GRPO
methods.data_it_needs: prompts each paired with a checkable ground-truth answer, since DAPO's reward is rule-based (`+1` for a verified match, `-1` otherwise), explicitly chosen over a learned reward model to avoid reward hacking
methods.extra_models: none beyond the policy
methods.when_to_pick: online RL with a rule-based or verifiable reward (not a learned reward model) on long chain-of-thought tasks, when a GRPO run shows entropy collapse or an increasing share of same-reward groups

methods.name: RLHF
methods.shipped_by: trl ships a `PPOTrainer`, but only under the experimental namespace `trl.experimental.ppo.PPOTrainer`, marked experimental in trl's own trainer taxonomy; the RM and SFT stages use trl's non-experimental `RewardTrainer` and `SFTTrainer`. verl's PPO is selected with `algorithm.adv_estimator: gae` (generalized advantage estimation, the same estimator InstructGPT's Appendix C.4 describes using with no discount) and requires a separate critic model, which verl's own docs contrast with GRPO and RLOO as not needing one
methods.variant_of: not a variant of a single named post-training method - RLHF is the parent framework here, built by applying RL from human preferences (carried into language-model fine-tuning for summarization by Stiennon et al.) as a three-stage SFT-then-RM-then-PPO pipeline, with PPO itself supplying the RL step unchanged
methods.data_it_needs: three separate datasets in the paper - an SFT set of about 13k prompts with labeler-written demonstrations; an RM set of about 33k prompts, each with K=4 to K=9 labeler-ranked model outputs, turned into $\binom{K}{2}$ pairwise comparisons per prompt; and a PPO set of about 31k prompts drawn only from the API, with no human labels attached, used purely to sample rollouts
methods.extra_models: three beyond the policy - the frozen SFT model used both as the PPO starting point and as the reference for the KL penalty; a reward model (6B parameters in the paper, shared across all policy sizes) that scores each rollout; and a PPO value network (also 6B, initialized from the reward model's weights) that provides the per-token baseline
methods.when_to_pick: pick RLHF when you can collect human comparisons over model outputs (or already have a trained reward model) and can afford an online RL loop that samples fresh completions from the current policy every step

methods.name: SIMPO
methods.shipped_by: trl, via `trl.experimental.cpo.CPOTrainer` with `loss_type="simpo"` — the docs list `CPOTrainer` under the "Experimental" section of the trainer index, alongside other loss-mode variants (CPO-SimPO, AlphaPO), rather than as a standalone top-level trainer
methods.variant_of: DPO
methods.data_it_needs: a preference dataset of (prompt, chosen response, rejected response) triples — the same shape DPO uses, no explicit reward model required
methods.extra_models: none by design — no reference model, no value network
methods.when_to_pick: offline preference optimization on chosen/rejected pairs when you want to drop the reference model entirely for memory and compute savings, and can tolerate an extra margin hyperparameter to tune

methods.name: IPO
methods.shipped_by: trl, as `loss_type="ipo"` inside the top-level `DPOTrainer` class exported by `trl`; no separate `IPOTrainer` class exists, IPO is one selectable loss within the general `DPOTrainer` (module `trl/trainer/dpo_trainer.py`, commit `2396dfe` on the `main` branch)
methods.variant_of: DPO, itself framed by the IPO paper as a special case of the same $\Psi$PO objective family that IPO belongs to
methods.data_it_needs: a dataset of prompts with a preferred and dispreferred completion per pair, $(x, y_w, y_l)$ - the same shape DPO consumes
methods.extra_models: one frozen reference policy $\pi_{ref}$, used both to initialize training and inside the loss's log-ratio term; trl's `DPOTrainer` loads this reference model for the `"ipo"` loss the same way it does for `"sigmoid"` DPO, since the loss is computed from the same chosen/rejected log-ratio quantities relative to a reference model
methods.when_to_pick: pick IPO over plain DPO when preference labels are likely to be sparse, imbalanced across actions, or close to deterministic (e.g. small per-prompt sample counts, one response winning or losing every comparison it appears in) - DPO's objective ignores the reference policy in these regimes and converges to a degenerate deterministic answer regardless of the KL strength, while IPO's bounded loss keeps the regularization strength $\tau$ in control of how far the policy moves

methods.name: REINFORCE
methods.shipped_by: no framework surveyed here ships a trainer literally implementing Williams's REINFORCE with a moving-average baseline
methods.variant_of: none — REINFORCE is the foundational stochastic policy-gradient algorithm in this corpus
methods.data_it_needs: prompts from the target task distribution and a scalar reward per sampled completion (a reward model or a programmable reward function); no preference pairs are required for the REINFORCE update itself
methods.extra_models: none required by the algorithm itself — Williams's original REINFORCE has no value network and no reference model
methods.when_to_pick: pick REINFORCE when every sampled completion can be scored with a scalar reward and the simplicity of having no critic and no clipped surrogate objective is the priority over the lower gradient variance that a group- or batch-relative baseline gives; Ahmadian et al.'s own results put plain REINFORCE-with-baseline behind their leave-one-out variant RLOO but ahead of a PPO baseline on the same reward models [2, Table 1]. Prefer RLOO or GRPO when multiple completions per prompt are affordable, since both replace the moving-average baseline with a same-batch or same-group baseline that Ahmadian et al. show reduces variance further

methods.name: DoRA
methods.shipped_by: Hugging Face PEFT, via `LoraConfig(use_dora=True)` (top-level `LoraConfig` export, current default `use_dora=False`; the config's own docstring warns DoRA currently only supports Linear and Conv2D layers and recommends merging weights before inference because of its larger runtime overhead). trl exposes the same setting as `ModelConfig.use_dora` / the `--use_dora` CLI flag on its training scripts, which it forwards into the `LoraConfig` it builds internally - trl does not implement DoRA itself
methods.variant_of: LoRA
methods.data_it_needs: whatever the underlying supervised fine-tuning task needs, since DoRA only changes how the weight update is parameterized, not the loss; the paper itself uses cross-entropy fine-tuning on prompt/answer pairs (commonsense reasoning, instruction tuning with a 10,000-example Alpaca subset) and a diffusion loss for text-to-image DreamBooth fine-tuning
methods.extra_models: none beyond whatever the base fine-tuning objective already requires (e.g. a reward model only if the surrounding pipeline uses one) - DoRA itself adds only a trainable magnitude vector per adapted matrix plus the usual LoRA $A$, $B$ matrices on top of the frozen pre-trained weight
methods.when_to_pick: pick DoRA over plain LoRA when the low-rank adapter is capacity-limited (small rank, or accuracy trailing full fine-tuning) and the extra per-column magnitude parameters and the one-time column-norm computation at adapter init are acceptable; the paper's own low-rank ablation is the deciding case (see How to use it)

methods.name: SFT
methods.shipped_by: trl, `SFTTrainer` / `SFTConfig`, contributed by Younes Belkada; verl, `verl.trainer.sft_trainer.SFTTrainer`, launched via Hydra with `config_name="sft_trainer_engine"` (read at commit reflected in the file fetched 2026-08-09)
methods.variant_of: none in the RL-method sense - SFT is the base supervised-learning technique that other post-training methods (RLHF, DPO, GRPO) are layered on top of, typically starting from an SFT checkpoint
methods.data_it_needs: (instruction, optional input, output) pairs, i.e. demonstrations of the desired behavior, not preference pairs or scalar rewards. trl's `SFTTrainer` accepts this as one of four column layouts: a single `text` field (plain language modeling), a `messages` field (conversational, chat-template applied automatically), a `prompt`/`completion` pair, or a conversational `prompt`/`completion` pair where each is a list of role/content turns
methods.extra_models: none
methods.when_to_pick: pick SFT whenever you have (or can curate) demonstrations of the exact behavior you want and no further preference or reward signal is available or needed; it is also the near-universal first stage before any RL or preference method, because RLHF and DPO pipelines almost universally start from an SFT-tuned model to establish a reasonable base policy

methods.name: RLVR
methods.shipped_by: no framework ships a trainer literally named "RLVR" — it is a reward-function convention (return 1/α for a verified-correct completion, 0 otherwise) applied on top of an existing on-policy trainer
methods.variant_of: the KL-constrained RLHF objective with a learned reward model, trained with online RL via PPO, with InstructGPT one instance of that RLHF objective, and with the reward model term $r_\phi(x,y)$ replaced by a deterministic verifier $v(x,y)$
methods.data_it_needs: prompts paired with a binary verifier function, not a scalar reward model or preference pairs
methods.extra_models: as PPO's objective, RLVR needs a value network (critic) and a frozen reference model for the KL term; no reward model is required for the verified reward itself, since $v(x,y)$ replaces it
methods.when_to_pick: online RL for tasks where a fixed, deterministic checker can grade a completion as correct or not (exact-match math, code execution, format/constraint following) and you want to skip training a reward model for that skill

methods.name: RAFT
methods.shipped_by: LMFlow (`lmflow.pipeline.raft_aligner.RaftAligner`, the toolkit built by the RAFT paper's own co-authors), but only conditionally - `AutoPipeline` in LMFlow's source registers `RaftAligner` under the key `raft_aligner` only when the installed `transformers` version is below 4.35.0, and otherwise leaves it unregistered (read at commit `ea19450`, 2026-08-09)
methods.variant_of: best-of-K (rejection) sampling, cited by the RAFT paper to WebGPT and Cobbe et al.; RAFT turns the inference-time best-of-K policy into an iterative training loop
methods.data_it_needs: a prompt set only - no chosen/rejected pairs, no per-token labels - plus a reward function that scores a completion given a prompt
methods.extra_models: a reward model to score completions (required); no value network, ever - the paper positions removing PPO's critic as a core reason for the method
methods.when_to_pick: when a reward model (or any scalar scorer) can score fresh completions and you want an alignment loop that only ever runs plain SFT - no critic, no clipped policy-gradient loss, no held reference model unless you opt into the KL-penalized ranking variant

methods.name: RLAIF
methods.shipped_by: no library ships a trainer named "RLAIF" - it is a labeling-source substitution layered on an existing RLHF pipeline, not a new loss
methods.variant_of: RLHF, with the AI-feedback substitution introduced as RLAIF by Bai et al
methods.data_it_needs: prompts from the target task distribution, matching the RLHF pipeline's own three phases
methods.extra_models: a reward model trained on AI-generated preferences (dropped entirely in d-RLAIF, where the off-the-shelf LLM scores rollouts directly); a value/baseline network for the REINFORCE policy gradient, initialized from the SFT model and trained alongside the policy; and an implicit frozen copy of the SFT policy used in the KL-penalty term of the RL objective
methods.when_to_pick: pick RLAIF over RLHF when the bottleneck is the cost or speed of collecting human preference labels - the paper estimates AI labeling at over 10x cheaper than Google Cloud's human annotation rate for its summarization setup ($0.06 vs. $0.67 per example) - and when an off-the-shelf LLM's preferences are an acceptable proxy for the target human judgments; the paper's own AI-labeler alignment with held-out human labels tops out around 78% (Table 3), so pick RLHF's parent pipeline directly when labeling accuracy against a specific human population is the priority

methods.name: ORPO
methods.shipped_by: LLaMA-Factory, as a stable, non-experimental training approach - its README lists ORPO alongside PPO, DPO, and KTO among its integrated methods, states it added ORPO support on 2024-03-31, and shows ORPO training with full-tuning, freeze-tuning, LoRA, QLoRA, OFT, and QOFT all checked in its supported-approaches table. trl also ships it, but only under the experimental namespace: `trl.experimental.orpo.ORPOTrainer` / `ORPOConfig`. trl's top-level `trl/__init__.py` does not export `ORPOTrainer` (read at commit `79842b8`, main branch, 2026-08-09); the trainer is importable only via `from trl.experimental.orpo import ORPOConfig, ORPOTrainer`. trl's own stability contract for that namespace states that "anything under trl.experimental may change or be removed in any release (including patch versions) without prior deprecation" and advises against relying on it "for production workloads". verl's documentation home page lists its algorithm pages (PPO, GRPO, DAPO, SPPO, GPG, entropy, and others) with no ORPO page among them, so this card treats verl as not shipping it (checked by fetching verl's docs index page, 2026-08-09)
methods.variant_of: not a strict derivative of one parent; the paper positions it against DPO as the other member of its "Alignment without Reward Model" family, contrasting its odds-ratio objective with DPO's and IPO's probability-ratio objective (paper's Eq. 16)
methods.data_it_needs: preference pairs - a prompt with a chosen and a rejected response per example, the same shape DPO consumes; no reward score, no reference-model logprobs are required at training time
methods.extra_models: none
methods.when_to_pick: preference pairs are available but you want to skip both the reward-model stage of RLHF/PPO and the frozen reference-model pass of DPO, at the cost of folding preference alignment into the SFT stage itself rather than running it after SFT. Nearest offline alternative and closest family relative is DPO, which needs a frozen reference model for its probability-ratio objective; ORPO needs none

methods.name: GSPO
methods.shipped_by: trl, via `GRPOTrainer` configured with `importance_sampling_level="sequence"` (there is no separate `GSPOTrainer` class); a GSPO-token variant ships as an experimental trainer under `trl.experimental.gspo_token.GRPOTrainer`. verl, via a registered policy-loss function `compute_policy_loss_gspo`, selected by setting `actor.policy_loss.loss_mode: "gspo"` (default is `"vanilla"`, i.e
methods.variant_of: GRPO, which is itself a variant of PPO
methods.data_it_needs: prompts from the target distribution plus a per-response scalar reward — the paper's own preliminaries define a query-response pair as scored by a verifier producing a reward in [0, 1], the same reward structure both GRPO and GSPO consume; the paper's own MoE runs used a cold-start model fine-tuned from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, with no query-set size, learning rate, or group size G given in the text
methods.extra_models: none required by the objective itself — like GRPO, GSPO has no value network
methods.when_to_pick: choose GSPO over its parent GRPO when training runs slightly off-policy (multiple gradient-update mini-batches drawn from one rollout batch, or repeated importance-sampling steps over the same batch) and, per the paper, especially for large or Mixture-of-Experts models, where GRPO's token-level ratio destabilizes training; trl's docs state the sequence-level ratio "only has an effect when training goes slightly off-policy... otherwise it is effectively equivalent to no modification". Prefer DPO when you have static chosen/rejected preference pairs and no way to score fresh samples: DPO trains offline on such pairs, with no reward model needed at training time

methods.name: SPIN
methods.shipped_by: no framework ships the paper's original algorithm as a top-level trainer. verl provides an experimental recipe (`recipe/spin`, kept in the separate `verl-recipe` git submodule, entry point `SpinTrainer` via `main_spin.py`) described as a recipe "inspired by" the SPIN paper rather than a reproduction of it — it substitutes iterative online DPO with dynamically-generated preference labels for the paper's fixed-target self-play. trl's current docs table of contents lists no SPIN trainer among its supported or experimental trainers
methods.variant_of: SFT, with a per-iteration loss that becomes DPO's pairwise objective under the logistic-loss choice, using the SFT ground truth as the fixed "chosen" side
methods.data_it_needs: only the existing SFT dataset $(x,y)$ pairs — prompt and a single ground-truth completion, no chosen/rejected pairs and no scalar reward column
methods.extra_models: by the paper's own definition, none beyond the single LLM being trained: the "opponent" is just a frozen copy of the same model's previous-iteration weights, reused as both the log-probability reference in the loss and the generator of rejected samples — no separate value network, reward model, or judge. verl's recipe, by contrast, does not reproduce this: because it replaces the fixed SFT target with online preference labeling, it requires an explicit reference policy (`ref_policy_wg`, periodically refreshed from the actor via `ref_update_freq`) and an optional reward-model config for ranking generations
methods.when_to_pick: pick SPIN when you have only an SFT dataset of prompt/response pairs — no preference labels, no reward model, and no budget to collect either — and you want a cheap iterative boost on top of SFT. Prefer plain DPO when you already have (or can afford to collect) real chosen/rejected preference pairs; DPO trains directly on those pairs in a single pass and needs no iterative generate-then-train loop

methods.name: RRHF
methods.full_name: Rank Responses to Align Language Models
methods.shipped_by: no major RL-post-training library was found to implement RRHF. Neither trl nor verl lists an RRHF trainer or advantage estimator in their source trees as read at commit-level snapshots below, and a GitHub repository-search for "RRHF" turned up no adopting framework besides the authors' own repository
methods.variant_of: PPO, per the paper's own framing of RRHF as a simplification of the PPO stage of RLHF
methods.data_it_needs: per prompt, k sampled responses (any mix of self-generated, other-LLM-generated, or human-authored) each with a scalar reward score; the official training script consumes one JSON object per line with fields `query`, `responses` (list), and `scores` (list)
methods.extra_models: none required by the method's own definition beyond the reward source used to score responses before training - no value network and no reference model, since the KL term is absent from the loss (Eq. 5)
methods.when_to_pick: offline alignment when you already have, or can cheaply generate, several ranked or reward-scored responses per prompt and want to avoid running PPO's four-model training loop

methods.name: REST
methods.shipped_by: no training-library trainer implements ReST-MCTS\* under this name
methods.variant_of: ReST$^{EM}$, which is itself a simplified, math/code-focused version of the general ReST framework
methods.data_it_needs: a set of problems with checkable final answers, at column level: a question, plus a ground-truth or oracle-verifiable correct answer used to prune and score generated traces
methods.extra_models: two trained models, not one
methods.when_to_pick: pick when the task has a checkable final answer (math/science problems with a ground-truth answer) and the goal is a higher-quality self-training set than plain outcome filtering, at the cost of running a tree search and training a second model online at every iteration

methods.name: SLIC
methods.full_name: show how the recently introduced Sequence Likelihood Calibration
methods.shipped_by: trl, as `loss_type="hinge"` inside the stable, top-level `DPOTrainer` (`from trl import DPOTrainer`)
methods.variant_of: SLiC
methods.data_it_needs: preference triples (x, y+, y-), plus SFT pairs (x, yref) for the cross-entropy regularization term
methods.extra_models: none required by the method's own objective - the calibration term uses the trained model's raw log-likelihoods of y+ and y-, and the regularization term is a plain cross-entropy to a fixed target sequence, not a KL against a stored reference-model copy
methods.when_to_pick: pick SLiC-HF when you already have, or can build, preference triples (x, y+, y-) and want an offline method that in its own definition needs no reward model, no value network, and no reference model at all - only the trained policy and a fixed regularization target

methods.name: PRIME
methods.shipped_by: verl, as an optional recipe (`recipe/prime`, entry point `main_prime.py` calling `RayPRIMETrainer`) hosted in the separately versioned `verl-project/verl-recipe` repository and pulled into verl as a git submodule, rather than one of verl's `examples/`-listed core trainers (PPO, GRPO, RLOO, DAPO are also recipe-only or core-listed on the same page, and PRIME sits in the recipe list)
methods.variant_of: not a single-parent variant — it is a reward-shaping layer usable with several policy-gradient algorithms; the paper's default instantiation is RLOO's leave-one-out advantage estimator, and the same paper reports plugging the same reward machinery into REINFORCE, GRPO, and PPO as well
methods.data_it_needs: prompts with a machine-checkable outcome verifier — LaTeX-matched answers for math or unit-test pass rates for code, no step-level labels — plus the rollouts sampled from the current policy each step
methods.extra_models: no value network
methods.when_to_pick: pick PRIME over plain outcome-only online RL when you have a cheap, per-response outcome verifier (e.g., an exact-match math checker or unit tests) and want denser, token-level credit assignment without collecting step labels or running a separate PRM training stage first; the paper's own ablation shows it beating outcome-only RLOO at matched training steps

methods.name: RSO
methods.shipped_by: no framework I checked implements RSO's rejection-sampling data-construction step. trl's `DPOTrainer` exposes `loss_type="hinge"`, which its own docs attribute to "the RSO authors" using a hinge loss on normalized likelihood from the SLiC paper, with `beta` playing the role of the reciprocal margin; reading `trl/trainer/dpo_trainer.py` at commit `85709ab` (main, fetched 2026-08-09) confirms the loss is `relu(1 - beta * delta_score)`, matching RSO's hinge-norm formula (Eq. 10)
methods.variant_of: DPO and SLiC; RSO reuses their loss functions and changes only the preference-pair construction step
methods.data_it_needs: a supervised fine-tuned (SFT) policy to sample from, a trained pairwise reward-ranking model to score and rank candidates, and prompts to sample completions for (from the SFT training distribution)
methods.extra_models: a pairwise reward-ranking model is required to score and rank the rejection-sampling candidates - RSO's definition depends on it, unlike DPO which has no reward model
methods.when_to_pick: pick RSO over plain DPO when you can afford to run an SFT policy plus a trained reward-ranking model to generate fresh preference pairs before each offline training run, and you want those pairs to approximate the reward-optimal policy rather than reusing whatever policy produced your raw preference data

methods.name: RFT
methods.shipped_by: no training library ships a dedicated "RFT" trainer as of this reading (checked trl's exported trainers - `SFTTrainer`, `DPOTrainer`, `GRPOTrainer`, `RLOOTrainer`, `KTOTrainer`, `RewardTrainer` - and its `trl/experimental` subpackage, and verl's `recipe` directory, neither lists an RFT/rejection-sampling-fine-tuning entry)
methods.variant_of: SFT; RFT and Online RFT sit in the same "Data Source / Reward Function / Gradient Coefficient" table entry pattern as SFT in DeepSeekMath's unified paradigm, differing from SFT only in dataset and gradient mask
methods.data_it_needs: a set of prompts/questions with a way to check correctness of a final answer (the paper used ~7,473 GSM8K training questions, each producing up to k=100 sampled reasoning paths at temperature 0.7 before filtering to distinct-equation-list paths)
methods.extra_models: none required by the paper's own method - no value network, no reward model, no separate reference model; correctness is checked by string/Python-equation matching against the known answer, not by a learned judge
methods.when_to_pick: pick RFT when you already have an SFT model, a rule-checkable correctness signal (final-answer match, unit tests, an executable checker), and want a cheap, RL-free way to squeeze more distinct correct reasoning paths out of that model without training a critic or reward model

methods.name: LCPO
methods.shipped_by: no framework ships LCPO as a built-in trainer or reward recipe as of this check - trl's `trainer/__init__.py` export list contains `DPOTrainer`, `GRPOTrainer`, `KTOTrainer`, `RewardTrainer`, `RLOOTrainer`, and `SFTTrainer`, with no length-control trainer among them, and verl's `recipe` collection (searched by directory name for "l1", "lcpo", and "length") also contains none
methods.variant_of: GRPO, via a reward-function change, not a change to GRPO's policy-gradient update
methods.data_it_needs: a dataset of prompt/final-answer pairs with no reasoning traces required - the paper trained on the DeepScaleR-Preview dataset, about 40K math question-answer pairs drawn from AIME, AMC, Omni-Math, and STILL. Each prompt is augmented at training time with a target-length instruction sampled uniformly from 100 to 4000 tokens; no length-labeled data is collected in advance
methods.extra_models: a frozen reference model for the KL term, and a correctness verifier (the paper uses a rule-based math-answer checker, not a learned reward model) - no value network, inherited from GRPO. The reference implementation (a fork of verl) trains with `use_kl_loss=True` and `kl_loss_coef=0.001`, which matches verl's own documented default KL loss coefficient of 0.001 rather than the DeepSeekMath paper's coefficient of 0.04
methods.when_to_pick: pick LCPO when you have a reasoning model already capable of long chain-of-thought and want inference-time control over how many tokens it spends, trading accuracy for latency on a per-request basis

methods.name: VERA
methods.shipped_by: `peft` (Hugging Face) exports `VeraConfig` and `VeraModel` from its top-level package; the docs carry no experimental or maintenance-mode marker for it
methods.variant_of: LoRA
methods.data_it_needs: whatever supervised data the underlying fine-tuning task needs — VeRA is not a preference- or reward-based method
methods.extra_models: none
methods.when_to_pick: pick VeRA over its parent LoRA when many task- or user-specific adapters must coexist in memory or be stored cheaply, since only the small scaling vectors (plus one shared seed) differ per adapter; do not pick it when adapted layers have widely different input/output shapes, because the single shared matrix pair must be sized for the largest layer and smaller layers waste that capacity

methods.name: OLORA
methods.shipped_by: no established training library was found to implement O-LoRA (continual learning) as a trainer
methods.variant_of: LoRA
methods.data_it_needs: a sequence of task datasets, each of ordinary instruction-formatted $(x,y)$ text pairs — the paper's standard benchmark uses five text-classification datasets reformatted as instructions, and its long-sequence benchmark combines 15 datasets drawn from that set plus GLUE and SuperGLUE. No replay buffer or stored past-task data is needed; task order is itself an experimental variable, and the paper reports results over 3 different orderings for each benchmark
methods.extra_models: none — no value network, reward model, or reference model
methods.when_to_pick: sequential instruction-tuning across a stream of tasks where past-task data cannot be stored or replayed (privacy, storage) and catastrophic forgetting must be controlled without training a full new model per task

methods.name: STEPGRPO
methods.shipped_by: no library implements StepGRPO - it does not appear in trl's or verl's trainer lists as of this reading
methods.variant_of: GRPO
methods.data_it_needs: two phases, both multimodal (image + text question)
methods.extra_models: no value network - inherited from GRPO. A frozen reference model is required by the method's own KL term (the paper's default coefficient is $\beta=0.04$, attributed to the trl library); both the policy and reference model are initialized from the post-warm-up checkpoint
methods.when_to_pick: online RL for MLLM step-by-step reasoning when outcome-only reward is too sparse for a weak or newly-warmed-up policy to learn from, and you have (or can extract with an LLM) a reference reasoning path to score intermediate steps against - StepGRPO's own motivation is exactly this sparse-reward regime

methods.name: STAR
methods.shipped_by: no RL or post-training library was found to ship a Quiet-STaR trainer; trl's GRPO trainer page, checked 2026-08-09, does not mention Quiet-STaR or STaR. The only available implementation is the original authors' research code at github.com/ezelikman/quiet-star (739 stars as of 2026-08-09), which the repository's own README describes as "implemented by simply patching the base Mistral implementation in Huggingface `transformers`" with a custom `modeling_mistral.py` and `configuration_mistral.py`, pinned to `transformers==4.37.0.dev0`, and otherwise using the standard Hugging Face `Trainer`
methods.variant_of: STaR (Self-Taught Reasoner)
methods.data_it_needs: unlabeled continuous text only - no prompts, no answers, no preference pairs, no reward-model scores
methods.extra_models: none in the sense of a separate value network, reference model, or reward model - the "reward" for REINFORCE is computed from the base model's own change in log-likelihood of the true continuation, with vs. without a rationale
methods.when_to_pick: pick Quiet-STaR only for research into giving a base LM an always-on reasoning habit via unsupervised continued pretraining on raw text, where no question/answer labels exist; it is not a chat- or instruction-tuning-stage method

methods.name: RLCS
methods.shipped_by: no released training framework implements RLCS's difficulty-tiered curriculum sampler as of this check (trl's `main`-branch GRPO trainer docs and verl's `latest` GRPO docs were both checked and neither mentions curriculum or difficulty-based sampling)
methods.variant_of: GRPO, itself a variant of PPO
methods.data_it_needs: multi-domain prompts covering both RLVR domains scored by rule- or model-based verifiers (Math, Physics, Chemistry, Long Document, Chart, OCR, general VQA, GeoGuess, Grounding, Spatial reasoning, GUI Agent, Video, per the paper's own reward-design table), and RLHF-style non-verifiable prompts (e.g. open-ended writing) scored by a text-based reward model for instruction compliance and fluency
methods.extra_models: no value network — that is inherited from GRPO. The paper explicitly discards the KL-loss term against a reference policy (finding it over-constrains capability growth in vision-language models) and discards an entropy-loss term (finding it caused garbled, collapsing outputs), so RLCS as run in this paper holds no frozen reference model and no extra entropy-regularization machinery
methods.when_to_pick: pick RLCS-style curriculum sampling when running large-scale, multi-domain online RL with per-sample verifiable or model-based rewards (GRPO/DAPO-style), specifically when rollout compute is the bottleneck and a fixed/uniform prompt-sampling distribution would waste that budget on prompts the policy already solves or cannot solve — the paper's own motivating case

methods.name: REFT
methods.shipped_by: neither trl nor verl implements a trainer named for ReFT; this card checked trl's top-level exports and verl's algorithms index, and neither lists it
methods.variant_of: PPO
methods.data_it_needs: warm-up stage needs (question x, CoT e, answer y) triples; the RL stage needs only (question x, answer y) pairs, since the CoT is sampled on-policy at each RL step
methods.extra_models: one value model, no reward model, and one frozen reference policy
methods.when_to_pick: online PPO for a reasoning task where an answer can be extracted and checked by a rule (exact match, or a program's output), so a reward model is unnecessary and the reward function can be used directly

methods.name: DYLORA
methods.shipped_by: no maintained library implements DyLoRA under a top-level export - Hugging Face PEFT's public API lists many LoRA variants (`LORA`, `ADALORA`, `XLORA`, `RANDLORA`, `DELORA`, `GRALORA`, `GLORA`, `VBLORA`, `UNILORA`, `TINYLORA`) but no DyLoRA entry, checked in `peft_types.py` and `__init__.py` at `main` on 2026-08-09
methods.variant_of: LoRA
methods.data_it_needs: whatever the base task needs - the paper's NLU experiments use the GLUE benchmark (labeled single-sentence and sentence-pair classification/regression data) and its NLG experiments use E2E, DART and WebNLG (structured input, target text pairs); DyLoRA adds no new data requirement over LoRA itself, only a choice of $r_{min}$/$r_{max}$ and a rank-sampling distribution $p_B$. Training is standard supervised fine-tuning on a fixed labeled dataset, not on-policy rollouts against a reward signal
methods.extra_models: none
methods.when_to_pick: pick DyLoRA when you want one LoRA-style adapter that can be deployed at several ranks (e.g. to trade accuracy for inference cost per-deployment) without retraining or without running a separate rank sweep; the paper's own evidence for this is the wide-range robustness in Table 2, especially the low-rank regime

methods.name: STARPO
methods.shipped_by: RAGEN (`ragen.trainer.agent_trainer.RayAgentTrainer`, subclassing verl's `RayPPOTrainer`) is the paper's own reference implementation and, as far as this card checked, the only shipping implementation of StarPO; it dispatches to GAE (PPO) or GRPO advantage estimation via a single `algorithm.adv_estimator` config key
methods.variant_of: generalizes PPO and GRPO from single-turn to trajectory-level optimization; not a single fixed variant of either
methods.data_it_needs: no fixed dataset of prompt-response or preference pairs
methods.extra_models: depends on which instantiation is used
methods.when_to_pick: pick StarPO when the training signal comes from a multi-turn, possibly stochastic environment (an agent that must act, observe a new state, and act again before a reward resolves) rather than from a single prompt-response pair

methods.name: FEDIT
methods.shipped_by: this card did not fetch or check trl, verl, OpenRLHF, or any other post-training library's docs or source for a FedIT trainer, so it makes no claim about whether one exists there; the only implementation this card found is the authors' own research repository, Shepherd (`JayZhang42/FederatedGPT-Shepherd`, Apache-2.0, 252 stars, last pushed 2023-07-07), which is a standalone client/server simulation script (`main.py`) rather than an adapter registered inside a larger training framework
methods.variant_of: FedAvg, specialized to LoRA-adapter-only local updates for LLM instruction tuning
methods.data_it_needs: per-client instruction-tuning records in the Alpaca prompt format used by the paper's repo -- an instruction, an optional input/context, and a response, filled into the "Prompt Input" / "Prompt No Input" templates given in Table 1 of the paper
methods.extra_models: none beyond the one shared base LLM. FedIT's definition trains a single global LLM whose weights are frozen while a LoRA adapter (matrices A and B) is trained locally and aggregated by FedAvg at the server; the paper reports the trainable LoRA parameters are 0.26% of the 7B base model's original parameter count (Table 2)
methods.when_to_pick: pick FedIT when instruction data must stay on separate devices or organizations for privacy or proprietary reasons, and you can accept a LoRA-only, FedAvg-averaged update rather than full-parameter training

methods.name: SPPO
methods.shipped_by: the paper's own reference implementation, `uclaml/SPPO`'s `SPPOTrainer` (subclass of a `Trainer`, `loss_type="sppo"` or `"sppo_single"`), 590 GitHub stars, Apache-2.0, last pushed 2025-01-23. trl's `DPOTrainer` supports `loss_type="sppo_hard"` as one of its documented, exported loss types — an approximation only: trl's own docs state it approximates the algorithm "by employing hard label probabilities, assigning 1 to the winner and 0 to the loser," dropping the paper's soft win-rate estimate and its use of more than 2 responses per prompt. verl has no SPPO support in its core package; a separately maintained community repository, `verl-project/verl-recipe`, ships an `sppo` recipe (`recipe/sppo`) built as a submodule against a pinned verl commit, but its actor implements a sequence-level regression toward a scalar reward-model score with a batch softmean baseline — mechanically different from both the paper's pairwise loss and trl's `sppo_hard` (see How it works and Cost)
methods.variant_of: DPO (same reference-model log-ratio parameterization; different loss target)
methods.data_it_needs: prompts only, no pre-collected pairs — SPPO generates its own completions each round
methods.extra_models: a frozen reference model $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ (the policy the current round starts from) is required by the loss's log-ratio term, exactly as in DPO. A preference model is also required to score sampled pairs — the paper uses PairRM, a 0.4B DeBERTa-V3 pairwise model — but this is an oracle input to data construction, not a model trained jointly with the policy, and it is not a value network: SPPO has no value network or per-token critic. verl's community recipe substitutes a scalar reward model plus a batch-level softmean baseline in place of PairRM (see Cost and How it works — this changes the algorithm's shape)
methods.when_to_pick: choose SPPO when you can query a pairwise (not necessarily transitive) preference oracle on demand for freshly sampled completions and want iterative, self-play-style improvement with a convergence guarantee toward a preference-game equilibrium rather than a fixed reward maximum

methods.name: MPO
methods.shipped_by: trl (`DPOTrainer` with `DPOConfig(loss_type=["sigmoid","bco_pair","sft"], loss_weights=[0.8,0.2,1.0])`) — trl's own docs name this exact combination as implementing MPO, and multi-loss support was merged into `main` on 2025-07-21
methods.variant_of: DPO, with BCO's quality loss and an SFT-style generation loss added as extra terms
methods.data_it_needs: preference pairs with a fixed schema — image, question, chosen response, rejected response per training example, no scalar reward column
methods.extra_models: one frozen reference model $\pi_0$, required by both the preference loss and the quality loss's implicit-reward term — a copy of the initial policy, forward passes only
methods.when_to_pick: offline preference tuning for a multimodal (image-conditioned) reasoning model when you have chosen/rejected response pairs and plain DPO on that data is known to degrade chain-of-thought generation quality or produce repetitive output

methods.name: VRPO
methods.shipped_by: no library implements VRPO training
methods.variant_of: DPO
methods.data_it_needs: offline preference pairs — a prompt $x$, a chosen completion $y_w$, and a rejected completion $y_l$ per row, exactly DPO's data shape; no fresh sampling from the current policy is required or used
methods.extra_models: one frozen reference model, exactly as in DPO — the paper initializes $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ from LLaDA 8B Instruct, the same checkpoint used to initialize the trained policy
methods.when_to_pick: pick VRPO specifically when preference-tuning a masked diffusion language model such as LLaDA, where exact log-likelihoods cannot be computed at all — it is not a competing choice among methods for autoregressive models, it is what makes DPO-style training on an MDM viable in the first place

methods.name: GRM
methods.shipped_by: no library implements SPCT's training pipeline (rejective-sampling cold start plus rule-based RL) as of this check — trl's GRPO trainer documentation makes no mention of generative or critique-based reward models. verl's live documentation search index (fetched directly, not the static search-results shell) does contain a page, its advanced "Reward Loop" guide, that supports calling an external Generative Reward Model (its own term, "GenRM") over an HTTP endpoint as one reward-source type alongside discriminative reward models, with a worked example that prompts a GenRM and parses a score from its text response; that page names neither SPCT nor this paper, and it is inference-time reward-scoring infrastructure, not an implementation of SPCT's RFT-plus-rule-based-RL training recipe
methods.variant_of: as an RM output format, a departure from the scalar/Bradley-Terry reward model; as an RL algorithm, an unmodified application of GRPO
methods.data_it_needs: a query plus one, two, or many candidate responses per example, with a ground-truth label identifying the best response (or, for a single response, a binary correct/incorrect ground-truth reward)
methods.extra_models: a frozen reference model for the GRPO KL term, inherited unmodified from GRPO's own formula; the paper reports grid-searching the KL coefficient over {0.00, 0.01, 0.02, 0.08} and using no separate format reward, instead relying on a larger KL coefficient to keep the output format stable
methods.when_to_pick: pick GRM+SPCT when the reward you need is for general, non-verifiable queries with no fixed rule or reference answer, and you want a reward model whose output you can sample and vote over at inference time instead of only at training time

methods.name: LOMO
methods.shipped_by: `transformers` `Trainer`, entry point `TrainingArguments(optim="lomo")` / `optim="adalomo"`, which dispatches to `lomo_optim.Lomo` / `lomo_optim.AdaLomo` - no deprecation or experimental marking found in the reviewed source. `accelerate`, entry point `Accelerator.lomo_backward(loss, learning_rate)`
methods.variant_of: SGD, with the paper's own theoretical case for why plain SGD is viable for LLM fine-tuning laid out in Sec. 3.1
methods.data_it_needs: whatever labeled or instruction-formatted fine-tuning data the task calls for; the method reads the same (input, target) batches any supervised fine-tuning loop reads
methods.extra_models: none
methods.when_to_pick: pick LOMO when the constraint is GPU memory for full-parameter fine-tuning of an LLM and Adam-style optimizer state (two full-precision moment buffers per parameter) does not fit, and when you are willing to hand-tune a plain-SGD-style learning rate instead of getting Adam's per-parameter adaptivity for free

methods.name: OPSD
methods.shipped_by: no library ships an `OPSDTrainer`
methods.variant_of: on-policy distillation (GKD), with the external teacher model replaced by the same weights under a different, privileged-information prompt
methods.data_it_needs: problem/reference-solution pairs $(x, y^\star)$, where $y^\star$ may include chain-of-thought reasoning — not preference pairs and not a scalar reward per answer
methods.extra_models: by the method's own definition (Eq. 1/8), no second model is needed — teacher and student are the same parameters $\theta$ under different conditioning
methods.when_to_pick: pick OPSD when every training prompt has a verified reference solution (an answer or a reference chain-of-thought), the base model is already capable enough to "rationalize" that reference when it is shown in context, and you want dense per-token supervision without paying for a second, larger teacher model or for GRPO-style multi-rollout groups

methods.name: TTRL
methods.shipped_by: the PRIME-RL/TTRL GitHub repository, the authors' own verl fork built for reproducing the paper's experiments, is the confirmed working implementation
methods.variant_of: not a new RL algorithm but a new reward function layered on an existing one; the paper's main experiments run it through GRPO, and it demonstrates compatibility with PPO and PRIME with closely aligned accuracy and entropy curves over training steps (Figure 5)
methods.data_it_needs: prompts only, no labels or preference pairs — a set of questions repeatedly sampled by the current policy
methods.extra_models: none beyond whatever the underlying RL algorithm requires — the paper's own text does not discuss a KL term or reference model for its GRPO runs at all; with the PPO variant, a learned state-value function is required, since PPO's own algorithm (given as "PPO, Actor-Critic Style") combines a policy surrogate loss with a value-function error term
methods.when_to_pick: pick TTRL when you have a batch of unlabeled prompts (often literally a benchmark's test split) that you can sample repeatedly, and you want the model to improve on that specific distribution without any ground-truth labels or reward model

methods.name: CODI
methods.shipped_by: no general-purpose post-training library ships a CODI trainer. trl's `trl/trainer` directory (18 files at the `main` branch as of this check) has no CODI-related entry. verl ships a generic `trainer/distillation` module (`losses.py`, plus fsdp/megatron backends) for output-level knowledge distillation, but it defines only generic distillation loss functions with no continuous-thought or teacher/student-same-weights mechanism, and does not name or implement CODI. A Hugging Face model search for "CODI" separately surfaces only the paper authors' own checkpoints and independent research forks, not a library entry point
methods.variant_of: Coconut's autoregressive continuous-thought mechanism, with Coconut's curriculum-learning training objective replaced by self-distillation
methods.data_it_needs: (question, chain-of-thought, answer) triples — the repository's data loader reads exactly these three fields (`question`, `cot`, `answer`) per example, reformatting the answer into an `"The answer is: <n>"` template and, for the default `icot` data mode, truncating the CoT by a fixed number of trailing steps per training example
methods.extra_models: none beyond the one model being trained
methods.when_to_pick: pick CODI when you have CoT-annotated training data (question, rationale, answer) and want a model that reasons internally with far fewer decoded tokens than explicit CoT, without the multi-stage curriculum-learning schedule Coconut needs and without training a separate reward or process-reward model

methods.name: REMAX
methods.shipped_by: verl, via `algorithm.adv_estimator=remax`; `compute_remax_outcome_advantage` in `verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py` implements the paper's advantage exactly and cites the paper's own arXiv ID in its docstring
methods.variant_of: REINFORCE (Williams, 1987; 1992), as the paper itself states; proposed as a lighter-weight, non-PPO alternative for the same RLHF Step-3 slot that PPO traditionally fills, not as a modification of PPO's own objective
methods.data_it_needs: a prompt-only dataset from the target distribution, plus any scoring function that returns one scalar reward per complete response — the paper's own RL stage used the full-hh-rlhf preference dataset's prompts (Llama-2-7B/OPT-1.3B experiments) and a mix of ultrafeedback, lmsys-chat-1m and sharegpt-en prompts at 10k/20k/40k scale (Mistral-7B experiments)
methods.extra_models: no value network, ever — this is the method's headline saving over PPO. A reward model (or equivalent scorer) is required to score both the sampled and the greedy response
methods.when_to_pick: pick ReMax when responses can be scored with a scalar reward (a reward model or a programmatic scorer) and you want an online, on-policy method without a value network and without PPO's clipped-ratio machinery — its own cost is one extra greedy-decode generation per prompt, not a second trained model

methods.name: SDPO
methods.shipped_by: only the paper's own code, `lasgroup/SDPO`, a repository the README states is built on top of a recent version of verl and which adds `actor.policy_loss.loss_mode = "sdpo"` plus an `actor.self_distillation` config block on top of that base
methods.variant_of: GRPO, which is itself a variant of PPO
methods.data_it_needs: prompts only, no pre-collected labels — SDPO samples G rollouts per prompt from the current policy each step, exactly like GRPO. It additionally needs a source of "feedback" text per rollout: either genuine environment output (compiler/runtime errors, the paper's coding experiments) or, when the environment returns only a scalar reward, another rollout in the same group that succeeded on the same question, used as an implicit sample solution
methods.extra_models: no separate value network and no explicit reward model — SDPO's advantage comes from the self-teacher, which is the same weights as the student, reprompted
methods.when_to_pick: pick SDPO over its parent GRPO when the environment already returns rich per-attempt feedback (compiler errors, unit-test tracebacks, judge rationales) and the base model is large enough to use that feedback in-context — the paper finds the gain over GRPO grows with model scale and can flip negative on a 1.5B model [1, Sec. 4.1]. Prefer on-policy distillation from an external teacher when a stronger model than the student is available to supervise it; SDPO is designed for the case where no such teacher exists and the model must supervise itself

methods.name: RLIF
methods.shipped_by: no production trainer library ships RLIF or Intuitor as of this reading; trl's and verl's package exports carry no RLIF/Intuitor entry point (checked against trl `main` `trl/__init__.py` and verl `main` `verl/trainer/__init__.py`, no match for "intuitor" or "rlif")
methods.variant_of: RLIF is presented as a paradigm parallel to RLHF and RLVR (exemplified by DeepSeek-R1), sharing their reward-plus-KL-penalty objective shape but replacing the reward term with an intrinsic signal
methods.data_it_needs: prompts only, no labels, no verifier, no preference pairs - the reward is computed from the policy's own token probabilities on its own sampled completion
methods.extra_models: a frozen reference model for the KL penalty ($\beta$ in Eq. 1), the same role GRPO's reference model plays; no value network (inherited from GRPO); no reward model and no verifier, since self-certainty is computed from the trained policy's own next-token distribution, not from a separate model
methods.when_to_pick: pick RLIF/Intuitor when you have prompts but no verifiable reward, gold answer, or preference labels, and the base model already has enough domain competence that its own confidence correlates with correctness - the paper's own failure-case analysis found training can collapse when this prior knowledge is inadequate

methods.name: DNO
methods.shipped_by: no library implements DNO. Checked at trl commit `dd7cbaf` (2026-07-31): the top-level `trl/__init__.py` exports only `DPOTrainer`, `GRPOTrainer`, `KTOTrainer`, `RewardTrainer`, `RLOOTrainer`, `SFTTrainer` — no Nash- or DNO-named trainer, and even trl's experimental folder (`trl/experimental/nash_md`) ships Nash-MD, not DNO. verl's algorithm documentation index lists `ppo`, `grpo`, `dapo`, `spin`, `sppo`, `dro`, `gpg`, `opd`, `opo`, `otb`, `entropy`, `baseline`, `rollout_corr`, `rollout_corr_math`, `dppo` — no DNO or Nash entry
methods.variant_of: DPO, run iteratively with on-policy resampling and preference-oracle-based pair construction; theoretically positioned as a batched, single-timescale approximation to the soft-policy-iteration updates that SPO uses to approach the Nash equilibrium of a general preference function
methods.data_it_needs: prompts only as the fixed dataset (the paper's main runs used UltraFeedback's ~60k prompts, split into three non-overlapping ~19.6-19.9k partitions, one per iteration; the scaled run used ~600k prompts from a mixture of six datasets)
methods.extra_models: no value network and, in the paper's own definition, no separately trained reward model — the preference judge is queried, not trained
methods.when_to_pick: pick DNO when you have query access to a pairwise or ranking preference oracle (a strong judge model, not a trained scalar reward model) and want DPO's training stability with fresh, on-policy self-improvement rounds instead of one fixed offline pair set

methods.name: LAT
methods.shipped_by: trl's documented trainer index (fetched from its `main` docs, 2026-08-09) lists no latent-adversarial-training trainer among its exported trainers (dpo, grpo, kto, reward, rloo, sft, bco, cpo, gkd, ppo, prm, xpo, and others)
methods.variant_of: untargeted LAT (Casper et al., 2024), itself a latent-space variant of PGD-based adversarial training (Madry et al., 2017)
methods.data_it_needs: a paired dataset of prompts with a desired (harmless/correct) completion and an undesired (harmful/target) completion, $(x_i, y_i, \tilde y_i) \sim D_p$, plus a separate benign dataset $D_b$ used to stabilize training via interleaved fine-tuning or a KL penalty
methods.extra_models: a reference/base copy of the model is needed only when the benign-preservation term is a KL penalty against the original weights, which the paper uses for its Llama-3 experiments (Llama-2 experiments instead interleave fine-tuning batches on the benign set, needing no extra model)
methods.when_to_pick: pick targeted LAT when you already have a training method (refusal training, DPO, gradient ascent, RMU) that is not fully removing a specific unwanted behavior (a backdoor, a jailbreak, a piece of forget-set knowledge) and you can specify what the undesired output looks like; it is added on top of that method's own loss, not a replacement for it

methods.name: GPO
methods.shipped_by: no framework ships a trainer literally named "GPO." trl's `DPOTrainer` implements three of the paper's named instances as a single `loss_type` config switch: `"sigmoid"` (DPO's logistic loss, the default), `"hinge"` (the SLiC-derived hinge loss), and `"ipo"` (IPO's squared loss); `from trl import DPOTrainer` is the entry point. verl's documentation index carries no GPO, IPO, or hinge-loss entries at all - only a DPO reference was found in a targeted index search on 2026-08-09
methods.variant_of: none in the sense of a single parent - GPO is the generalization, with DPO as the instance it most directly builds its derivation around; IPO and SLiC are the other two named special cases
methods.data_it_needs: offline pairwise preference data - a prompt with a chosen (win) and rejected (loss) response per example, collected without any live sampling from the model being trained
methods.extra_models: a frozen reference policy $\pi_{ref}$ is required by every GPO variant's log-ratio term, exactly as in DPO; no separate reward model or value network is trained, since the reward is implicitly parameterized through the policy's own log-ratio to the reference
methods.when_to_pick: pick GPO as an analysis lens, not as a single trainer to reach for - it tells you that DPO, IPO, and SLiC are one family with a shared derivation, so choosing among them is choosing a convex function $f$ and its matching $\beta$, not choosing between unrelated algorithms

methods.name: SPO
methods.shipped_by: no library implements it. `trl`'s trainer directory (as of the 2026-08-09 fetch) exports `dpo`, `grpo`, `kto`, `reward`, `rloo`, and `sft` trainers and no self-play or SPO trainer
methods.variant_of: the two-policy dueling technique for computing Minimax Winners (Yue et al., 2012, cited via) — SPO's contribution is proving a single self-play agent against its own past iterates suffices, removing the second policy
methods.data_it_needs: query access to a preference function $P: \Xi \times \Xi \to [-1,1]$ over pairs of trajectories, anti-symmetric ($P(\xi_1,\xi_2) = -P(\xi_2,\xi_1)$) and zero on ties ($P(\xi,\xi)=0$) — either a preference model trained offline (RLAIF-style) or a human-in-the-loop rater
methods.extra_models: no reward model and no second dueling policy by SPO's own definition
methods.when_to_pick: online RL when you have query access to a preference function over pairs of trajectories (a human rater or an AI comparator) and want to avoid both training a reward model and the instability of two-policy adversarial dueling, especially when preferences may be intransitive, non-Markovian, or aggregated across raters with disagreement

methods.name: DPA
methods.shipped_by: no library ships DPA as a named trainer
methods.variant_of: Rejection Sampling Fine-tuning / RAFT, made preference-conditional and multi-objective
methods.data_it_needs: (a) reward-model training data: prompt-response pairs with multi-attribute human or model ratings — the paper used HelpSteer (10K prompts, 37K responses, 5 attributes, 0-4 human ratings) and UltraFeedback (64K prompts, 4 responses each, 5 attributes, GPT-4 ratings); (b) fine-tuning data: prompts only (UltraFeedback prompts in the paper), no chosen/rejected pairs needed, since responses and their rankings are generated by the policy itself at each iteration
methods.extra_models: a multi-objective reward model is required by the method's own definition — it scores every sampled response on k attributes before ranking; the paper's reward model is Mistral-7B with a linear regression head
methods.when_to_pick: pick DPA when you need one deployed model that a user can steer along a continuous trade-off between two or more reward objectives at inference time (e.g., dial down verbosity without a separate model), and you already have or can train a multi-objective reward model

methods.name: TDPO
methods.shipped_by: no established framework
methods.variant_of: DPO
methods.data_it_needs: the same triples as DPO — a prompt $x$ and a preferred/dispreferred completion pair $(y_w, y_l)$, no per-token or per-step labels beyond that pairing
methods.extra_models: one frozen reference model $\pi_{ref}$, the same requirement as DPO — no value network and no separate reward model at training time, because the reward is implicit in the policy/reference log-ratio, as in DPO. Every token-level forward pass needs $\pi_{ref}$'s per-token vocabulary distribution (not just its log-prob of the sampled token), because the forward-KL term sums over the whole vocabulary at each position — see How it works and Cost
methods.when_to_pick: offline preference fine-tuning, same setting as DPO (a fixed dataset of preferred/dispreferred pairs, no reward model, no sampling loop), when DPO's training runs show the entropy/diversity collapse the paper documents and a tighter per-token KL trade-off is wanted; TDPO adds no new data requirement over its parent, DPO, and stays offline, unlike PPO-style online RLHF, which needs a reward model and fresh rollouts each step and is the paper's own PPO/trlx baseline in its MT-Bench comparison

methods.name: PRORL
methods.full_name: Prolonged Reinforcement Learning Expands Reasoning Boundaries in Large Language Models
methods.shipped_by: no library ships a "ProRL" trainer
methods.variant_of: GRPO, with DAPO's decoupled clipping and dynamic sampling folded in
methods.data_it_needs: prompts with a programmatically verifiable reward, no chosen/rejected pairs and no learned reward model - the paper's 136K-example mix uses answer matching for math, test execution for code, and rule-based constraint checking (IFEval-style) for instruction following
methods.extra_models: no value network (inherited from GRPO); one frozen reference policy for the KL term, which the method's own definition requires to be periodically hard-reset - weights and optimizer state - to a recent snapshot of the online policy, monitored via a held-out validation blend
methods.when_to_pick: pick ProRL when you plan to run RL for thousands of steps (the paper ran past 2k) to push a model's reasoning boundary rather than a few hundred steps to sharpen it, particularly when starting from a weaker base model - the paper finds the biggest pass@128 gains where the base model's initial reasoning boundary is lowest

methods.name: GPG
methods.shipped_by: verl, via `algorithm.adv_estimator: gpg` plus `actor_rollout_ref.actor.policy_loss.loss_mode: "gpg"`, listed under verl's "Algorithm Baselines" heading without an experimental or maintenance-mode label. trl does not implement GPG: its top-level package `__init__.py` (fetched revision) exports no GPG-named trainer
methods.variant_of: GRPO, with the clipped surrogate objective, KL-vs-reference term, and std-based reward normalization removed and a gradient debiasing factor added
methods.data_it_needs: prompts (question, ground-truth answer) with a rule-based accuracy reward (1.0 correct / 0.0 incorrect) as the main experiments' reward signal, plus an optional formatting reward and an IoU reward for a grounding task
methods.extra_models: none required by the method's own definition — Table 2 in the paper marks GPG as having no value model, no reference model, no surrogate loss, and no policy constraint, the only one of PPO/GRPO/TRPO/GPG with all four off. verl's documented "Advanced Extensions" for GPG show an optional KL-loss add-on (`use_kl_loss: True`, `kl_loss_coef: 0.01`) that reintroduces a frozen reference model, but verl's own global actor default has `use_kl_loss: false` (a live `main`-branch read of `verl/trainer/config/actor/actor.yaml`, not pinned to a commit hash and not independently dated by verl's docs), so no reference model loads unless that flag is set
methods.when_to_pick: on-policy RL for LLM reasoning when every sampled completion gets a single scalar outcome reward and you want to avoid GRPO's extra reward-std normalization, clip term, and KL-regularized reference model — the paper's own Table 1 shows GPG's final configuration beating or matching GRPO on all five reported math benchmarks under matched hyperparameters, including a tie on AMC23 (62.5 vs 62.5) alongside gains on AIME24 (30.0 vs 16.7), MATH-500 (76.2 vs 73.4), Minerva (34.2 vs 30.2), and OlympiadBench (39.0 vs 35.7)

methods.name: WARM
methods.full_name: we propose Weight Averaged Reward Models
methods.shipped_by: no WARM implementation was found in trl or verl, the two libraries checked for this card; other RLHF/post-training libraries were not searched
methods.variant_of: prediction ensembling of reward models, replacing logit averaging with weight averaging in the style of model soups, applied to RMs trained with the standard Bradley-Terry loss
methods.data_it_needs: a preference dataset of (prompt, chosen response, rejected response) triples, the same format used to train a single Bradley-Terry reward model
methods.extra_models: none beyond what the M underlying RM fine-tuning runs each require — each of the M runs starts from the same SFT checkpoint plus a linear-probed classifier head, and the M resulting weight sets are averaged offline into a single deployed RM, so no extra model is held or loaded at reward-inference or RL time
methods.when_to_pick: pick WARM when you are training a reward model for RLHF from a shared pretrained/SFT checkpoint, want the reliability benefits of ensembling multiple RMs, and cannot afford to keep M models loaded at inference time for reward scoring during RL. Its nearest offline alternative is a single reward model trained once by minimizing the Bradley-Terry negative log-likelihood, the standard RLHF recipe WARM builds on; its nearest online neighbor is prediction ensembling (ENS), which averages the logits of M separately trained RMs at inference time instead of their weights, keeping all M models loaded and paying inference cost that grows linearly with M

methods.name: SCOTT
methods.shipped_by: no post-training library implements SCOTT as a ready trainer; the authors' own PyTorch research code (`consistent-CoT-distillation`) is the only implementation, with separate scripts for contrastive-decoding data generation and counterfactual-training fine-tuning, unaccompanied by a stated support status
methods.variant_of: rationale-distillation knowledge distillation in the self-rationalization paradigm (student generates a rationale, then predicts conditioned on it), as opposed to post-rationalization (predict then explain) or multi-task rationale generation, a framing SCOTT's own paper uses to distinguish itself from Li et al. and Shridhar et al
methods.data_it_needs: for the teacher step, a handful of hand-written few-shot exemplars, each a question, gold answer, and a human-written rationale, used as an in-context prompt; and a training set of question-answer pairs (no rationales required) for the teacher to rationalize over - the paper used CSQA, StrategyQA, CREAK, and QASC, with official dev sets repurposed as test sets since test labels are not public
methods.extra_models: a frozen teacher LM for rationale generation - the paper uses GPT-NeoX-20B, chosen because the checkpoint is public and exposes token-wise probabilities needed for contrastive decoding; no reward model and no value network
methods.when_to_pick: pick SCOTT when you need a small model that both answers and emits a rationale, and you specifically care that the rationale is faithful to the model's own decision (measured by LAS, not just task accuracy)

methods.name: SDFT
methods.shipped_by: trl, under `trl.experimental.sdft` (`SDFTConfig`, `SDFTTrainer`)
methods.variant_of: on-policy distillation
methods.data_it_needs: per example, a prompt $x$ and a demonstration $c$ (TRL's dataset schema names these columns `prompt` and `privileged_context`); no reward, no chosen/rejected pair, no explicit label beyond the demonstration text itself
methods.extra_models: the definition always needs a second scored distribution, $\pi(\cdot/x,c)$, but the paper is explicit that this need not be separate weights: "unless mentioned otherwise, we use an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student parameters for the teacher", and the paper's own Algorithm 1 updates the teacher parameters $\phi \leftarrow \alpha\theta + (1-\alpha)\phi$ every step — one extra weight-sized copy held in memory, no gradients
methods.when_to_pick: expert demonstrations exist but no scalar reward does, and you want to add a skill without eroding prior capabilities — SDFT is not a substitute for on-policy RL but a complementary regime for exactly this supervision gap, per the paper's own Discussion

methods.name: DPG
methods.shipped_by: no packaged training library implements DPG. Checked trl's trainer directory listing (`base_trainer.py`, `dpo_trainer.py`, `grpo_trainer.py`, `kto_trainer.py`, `reward_trainer.py`, `rloo_trainer.py`, `sft_trainer.py` — no DPG entry) and verl's own documentation site index, which lists its algorithm pages as baseline, dapo, dppo, dro, entropy, gpg, grpo, opd, opo, otb, ppo, rollout_corr, rollout_corr_math, spin and sppo, with no "dpg" entry, both as of 2026-08-09; neither exports a DPG trainer
methods.variant_of: Policy Gradient / REINFORCE (Williams, 1992), as cited by the DPG paper
methods.data_it_needs: no labeled dataset in the conventional sense; the paper's setup needs an unnormalized target potential $P(x)$ and an initial proposal policy $q$ (in the paper's synthetic experiments, $q$ is a standard autoregressive model $r$ pretrained on the same domain)
methods.extra_models: none beyond the trained policy and the proposal $q$ used for sampling — $q$ is not gradient-trained, only used for sampling and occasionally replaced by a copy of the current policy
methods.when_to_pick: pick DPG when the thing you want the policy to match is a distribution given as an unnormalized potential $P(x)$ (an energy-based model or a set of pointwise/distributional constraints) rather than a per-sample scalar reward to be maximized, and you can sample from a reasonable proposal policy $q$. The nearest offline alternative is distillation, which the DPG paper directly compares against on the same synthetic task and finds comparably effective when the target can be sampled directly, but distillation requires being able to draw exact samples from the target and cannot be applied when the target is given only as an unnormalized potential

methods.name: ARPO
methods.shipped_by: no mainline framework ships ARPO — a case-insensitive text search for "arpo" in trl's GRPOTrainer documentation page and verl's GRPO algorithm documentation page, both read 2026-08-09, returned zero matches in either file
methods.variant_of: GRPO, restated inside the ARPO paper with the same clipped surrogate, group-normalized advantage, and reference-policy KL term
methods.data_it_needs: prompts paired with a checkable final answer, scored during RL by a piecewise reward built from format compliance, answer accuracy, and a multi-tool-use bonus (defined exactly in How to use it), not by a plain exact-match/F1 score — the paper's RL phase used 10K Tool-Star reasoning/knowledge prompts for the deep-reasoning setting and only 1K mixed hard-search prompts (from SimpleDeepSearcher and WebSailor) for the deep-search setting
methods.extra_models: no value network, inherited from GRPO's group-baseline design
methods.when_to_pick: online RL for training an LLM agent that calls external tools (search, browser, code) across multiple turns, when the reward is scored at the end of a trajectory (exact-match or F1 against a ground-truth answer in the paper's setup) and you want exploration concentrated at the specific tool-call steps where the policy is most uncertain, rather than spread evenly across whole trajectories

methods.name: LISA
methods.shipped_by: axolotl, config keys `lisa_n_layers` and `lisa_step_interval` (plus `lisa_layers_attribute`, default `model.layers`), read from `src/axolotl/utils/schemas/integrations.py` and wired into the trainer via `lisa_callback_factory` in `src/axolotl/utils/callbacks/lisa.py`, tree read at commit `93dcd622f1ceddaabce272569736ec0f205fba4d` on `main`
methods.variant_of: not a formal variant of LoRA — the paper presents it as an alternative to LoRA — but algorithmically it is AdamW full-parameter fine-tuning with a random layer-freezing schedule layered on top, so its true parent is full-parameter AdamW training
methods.data_it_needs: any labeled fine-tuning set (prompt/response pairs, e.g. the paper's 52K-pair Alpaca-GPT4 instruction data) or plain unlabeled text for continued pretraining (the paper used a 1.5-billion-token OpenWebMath subset); there is no reward or preference-pair requirement, since training is ordinary supervised next-token or instruction-tuning loss
methods.extra_models: none
methods.when_to_pick: pick LISA for supervised or continued-pretraining fine-tuning of a single model on labeled or plain-text data when you want full-parameter-level quality on a LoRA-level memory budget, especially on models too large to fully fine-tune (the paper scales to LLaMA-2-70B)

methods.name: SKTUNING
methods.shipped_by: no packaged training library implements SK-Tuning — a search of trl's live `main`-branch documentation index page (huggingface.co/docs/trl, fetched 2026-08-09) found no reference to "self-knowledge," "SK-tuning," or "self-eval" trainers; this covers only that page's current, unpinned build, not any release version of trl
methods.variant_of: a reference-free special case of DPO's pairwise loss
methods.data_it_needs: True/False question-answer pairs, self-generated and self-labeled, not collected from humans
methods.extra_models: by the paper's own equation, none — no value network, no reference model, no reward model; SK-Tuning trains the policy directly on its own two-token log-probabilities
methods.when_to_pick: pick SK-Tuning only as a preparatory stage inside a self-alignment-for-factuality pipeline, when you want to reduce hallucinations without human factuality annotations and are willing to run two fine-tuning stages (calibration, then DPO) instead of one

methods.name: RPO
methods.shipped_by: trl, via `DPOConfig(loss_type=[...], loss_weights=[...])` on the exported `DPOTrainer`/`DPOConfig` pair (both top-level package exports) - not a dedicated `RPOTrainer` class, but trl's own paper index gives RPO a named reproduction recipe on `main`; the page states no separate support/maintenance status for this recipe. verl's documentation has no DPO or RPO page at all (its `/algo/dpo.html` returns a 404, and no "dpo" or standalone "rpo" trainer name appears in its docs index), so verl does not ship this method; building it there would mean writing a DPO-style pairwise loss (plus one SFT NLL term) on top of verl's actor-training loop rather than its RL rollout loop, since RPO needs no rollout sampling
methods.variant_of: DPO
methods.data_it_needs: an offline preference dataset of prompt, chosen-response, rejected-response triples - trl's DPOTrainer accepts this as `{"prompt", "chosen", "rejected"}` fields in standard or conversational format, the same schema DPO uses
methods.extra_models: one frozen reference model, required by the DPO term the same way DPO itself requires one - trl's DPOTrainer creates a copy of the model at the start as the reference if none is passed
