methods.when_to_pick: offline preference optimization when you already have static chosen/rejected pairs and specifically want a cheap defense against DPO's overoptimization symptom (declining chosen-response likelihood during training) - the paper reports RPO fixes this without extra preference data or a changed training pipeline

methods.name: TORL
methods.shipped_by: no framework ships a trainer named ToRL. The paper's own reference implementation is the GAIR-NLP/ToRL GitHub repository, which is not a GitHub fork of verl (its own repository metadata records `fork: false`) but bundles a full copy of verl inside the repo and patches `verl/workers/rollout/vllm_rollout/vllm_rollout_spmd.py` to call an external Sandbox Fusion server mid-rollout; it is launched via a training script rather than an installable package entry point
methods.variant_of: GRPO, with the policy-update math untouched and the rollout/reward changed
methods.data_it_needs: prompts only, each with a checkable final answer, no chosen/rejected pairs or step-level annotations
methods.extra_models: none beyond the policy being trained
methods.when_to_pick: pick ToRL's rollout-and-reward pattern when the task is machine-verifiable (a checkable final answer, as in competition math) and precise computation is the bottleneck for a pure chain-of-thought policy, and you are willing to run RL directly from a base model rather than an instruction-tuned one

methods.name: DART
methods.shipped_by: no RL or SFT training library (trl, verl, axolotl) exposes a `DARS`/DART trainer
methods.variant_of: rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT), specifically the "vanilla rejection tuning" baseline defined and used for comparison in the DART paper
methods.data_it_needs: a set of math queries with ground-truth final answers (the paper fixes GSM8K and MATH training queries), plus a generator model to sample candidate responses (DeepSeekMath-7B-RL in the paper, an open-weight 7B model, explicitly avoiding GPT-4)
methods.extra_models: none beyond the response generator used at data-synthesis time (frozen, inference-only, no gradients)
methods.when_to_pick: pick DART over plain rejection sampling / RFT whenever the correct-response yield differs a lot by query difficulty, since a fixed per-query trial budget under-samples exactly the hard queries needed for reasoning gains, and DART's own ablation shows this data-distribution fix outperforming a same-size VRT baseline by up to ~7 points on MATH. It is an offline, SFT-only method: all training data is generated once, up front, from a fixed policy snapshot (DeepSeekMath-7B-RL in the paper) and then used for standard supervised fine-tuning, unlike online RL training, which resamples from the current policy during the run

methods.name: GDPO
methods.shipped_by: verl, as an advantage estimator (`algorithm.adv_estimator=gdpo`, function `compute_gdpo_outcome_advantage` in `verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py`, registered under `AdvantageEstimator.GDPO`), paired with a dedicated reward manager (`reward.reward_manager.name=gdpo`, class `GDPORewardManager`) that verl currently ships under its experimental reward-loop path (`verl/experimental/reward_loop/reward_manager/gdpo.py`), not the stable trainer path. verl's example script and README for this recipe are at `examples/gdpo_trainer/`. trl also ships it natively inside its existing `GRPOTrainer`, not as a separate trainer: `GRPOConfig(multi_objective_aggregation="normalize_then_sum")` switches the trainer's multi-reward aggregation from its default (sum the weighted per-function rewards, then normalize once) to GDPO's per-function group normalization followed by a batch-level whitening pass, implemented directly in `_generate_and_score_completions`. trl's own config docstring names this option as the paper's own suggested approach
methods.variant_of: GRPO, itself a variant of PPO
methods.data_it_needs: prompts plus, for each rollout, a vector of per-reward-dimension scalar scores (e.g. a format score and a correctness score), not a single pre-summed reward — GDPO's advantage estimator requires the individual reward keys to normalize each one within the group before summing
methods.extra_models: none required by the method's own definition beyond what GRPO needs — no value network, since GDPO only changes how the group-relative advantage is computed from already-scored rollouts
methods.when_to_pick: pick GDPO over plain GRPO specifically when training against two or more reward components at once (e.g., accuracy plus format, or accuracy plus a length constraint) and the components can trade off against each other; the paper's own ablation shows that GRPO's single normalization of the summed reward can silently erase which component drove a given total, and that removing GRPO's std term (Dr.GRPO-style) does not fix it, since that variant converged correctness but produced 0% correct-format compliance in the tool-calling task while GDPO reached 80.66%. For a single scalar reward, GDPO reduces to running GRPO per-dimension on one dimension plus an added batch-level whitening step, so plain GRPO is the simpler choice

methods.name: LIPO
methods.shipped_by: no library implements the general LiPO-λ listwise objective (Eq. 10, K responses, the $\Delta_{i,j}$ Lambda weight)
methods.variant_of: DPO, generalized from pairwise (K=2) to listwise (K≥2) preference data via a Learning-to-Rank objective
methods.data_it_needs: for each prompt x, a list of K responses $\{y_1,...,y_K\}$ with graded relevance labels $\psi = \{\psi_1,...,\psi_K\} \in [0,1]$ (win-probability scores against the rest of the list, not just a rank order)
methods.extra_models: a frozen reference policy $\pi_{ref}$ (the SFT checkpoint), required by the score definition itself for every loss variant in the framework, no exception
methods.when_to_pick: pick LiPO-λ over DPO when your preference data is already collected as a ranked list of more than two responses per prompt (e.g., from a reward model scoring several sampled completions) and you want to use the whole list instead of subsampling pairs

methods.name: SGRPO
methods.shipped_by: no framework implementation found
methods.variant_of: GRPO
methods.data_it_needs: prompts with a rule-checkable correct answer (no preference pairs, no learned reward model)
methods.extra_models: none
methods.when_to_pick: pick S-GRPO when you are already running outcome-reward RL (GRPO) on a reasoning model with a rule-checkable answer format and want to shorten CoTs without a separate accuracy-reducing length penalty; it costs extra rollouts per prompt (one full CoT plus several early-exit continuations) that plain GRPO does not need

methods.name: BPO
methods.shipped_by: a GitHub repository-name/description search for "bootstrapped preference optimization" and "BPO" returns exactly one result, the authors' own repository, and trl's DPOTrainer docs page contains no mention of BPO — GitHub's code-search API (which would find a `BPOTrainer`-style class inside another framework's source) requires authentication not available in this session, so this is a repo-level search only, not a code-level one

methods.extra_models: a frozen reference policy $\pi_0$ (the DPO KL-anchor, here the LLaVA1.5 checkpoint before BPO tuning), required by the objective exactly as in DPO — no value network, no separate reward model

methods.name: VPD
methods.shipped_by: no library implements VPD. A GitHub repository search for "visual program distillation" returns only the paper's own project-website repository, which carries no training code and has 0 stars
methods.variant_of: ViperGPT's visual-program framework, trained with the label-plus-rationale dual-loss recipe of Distilling Step-by-Step
methods.data_it_needs: (image, textual query, short expected-answer label) triples from academic VQA-style datasets

methods.name: MAPORL
methods.full_name: Multi-Agent Post-co-training for collaborative LLMs with Reinforcement Learning
methods.shipped_by: no established RL post-training library (TRL, verl, or similar) ships MAPoRL as a built-in trainer
methods.variant_of: multi-agent PPO, itself an extension of PPO
methods.data_it_needs: prompts/questions only for the RL stage — MAPoRL needs no chosen/rejected pairs and, given a sufficiently reliable verifier, no answer labels, since the verifier substitutes for gold answers
methods.extra_models: a verifier model is required by the method's own definition — a quantized LLM backbone with a linear head and softmax so its score falls in [0,1], trained separately from the RL stage on held-out data
methods.when_to_pick: pick MAPoRL when the goal is specifically to train LLMs to collaborate better in a multi-turn, multi-agent debate — not merely to raise single-model task accuracy — and a scalar verifier (or reward model) can score each turn's answer

methods.name: RAFE
methods.shipped_by: no library ships "RaFe" as a named trainer; it is a training recipe (reranker score -> DPO/KTO/PPO) built on existing trainers
methods.variant_of: DPO, KTO, and PPO (RaFe is the same three algorithms with the reward/preference label replaced by a reranker score; it does not change any of their objectives)
methods.data_it_needs: for the SFT stage, query/query-rewrite pairs produced by prompting an LLM (the paper used Qwen-max to produce rewrites for six QA datasets spanning English: HotpotQA, TriviaQA, NQ, and Chinese: baike, webqa, sougouqa, squadzen, balle, coig, totaling 123,500 instances by summing Table 6's own per-dataset counts: EN hotpotqa 12,471 + triviaqa 28,083 + nq 19,445 = 59,999; ZH baike 6,552 + webqa 16,486 + sougouqa 9,488 + squadzen 6,294 + balle 9,601 + coig 15,080 = 63,501)
methods.extra_models: a frozen reranker used only for scoring, never fine-tuned - the paper uses the public BAAI/bge-reranker-base
methods.when_to_pick: pick RaFe when you are training a small query-rewriting model for RAG and want a reward/preference signal without labeled relevant documents or answers; a public reranker's ranking score over the rewrite's retrieved documents stands in for that label

methods.name: VDPO
methods.shipped_by: no library implements V-DPO. The paper's own reference code is a standalone research repository (`YuxiXie/V-DPO` on GitHub, Apache-2.0, 60 stars as of this check) built as a fork of the LLaVA codebase, with the loss implemented in `llava_dpo/train/dpo_train.py` and run via `scripts/v1_5/vdpo.sh` - a script-based training pipeline, not an installable package with an exported trainer class. trl's own documentation table of contents lists DPO, Online DPO, and SDPO trainers but no vision-guided or V-DPO variant
methods.variant_of: DPO
methods.data_it_needs: image-conditioned preference pairs $(v, x, y_w, y_l)$ - an image, a query, a preferred response, and a dispreferred response - drawn from either "response-contrast" pairs (same image, different responses) or the paper's own "image-contrast" pairs (same response, different images, constructed by swapping visual elements in an image with unexpected substitutes)
methods.extra_models: one frozen reference model $\pi_{ref}$, the same as vanilla DPO, needed to compute the log-ratio term in the loss
methods.when_to_pick: offline preference training for an LVLM when hallucination stems from the model ignoring the image and defaulting to text-only priors, and you can construct or reuse image-conditioned preference pairs

methods.name: PM
methods.shipped_by: no library implementation was found
methods.variant_of: standard KL-regularized RLHF, which the paper attributes to InstructGPT, with the KL-to-reference term replaced by the PM regularizer
methods.data_it_needs: the same data RLHF's reward-maximization stage needs - a prompt set plus a trained scalar reward model $r_\theta(x,y)$; the paper's own experiments split the human-preference dataset 20% for SFT, 40% for reward-model training, and 40% for the reward-maximization stage, and use PPO to run that stage
methods.extra_models: one frozen reference model, used two ways in the practical (conditional) variant - to define which responses get the ordinary PM penalty versus the pull-toward-reference penalty (via the threshold $\alpha$), and as the resampling baseline $\pi_{ref}(y/x)$ inside that penalty; plus the reward model needed for any RLHF reward-maximization stage
methods.when_to_pick: a research or fairness-auditing setting where the reward model itself encodes graded, non-unanimous preferences (e.g. a 60%/40% split between two responses) and the goal is for the fine-tuned policy's own output probabilities to reproduce that split rather than collapse to the majority answer; the paper positions this against ordinary KL RLHF, which it proves does not have this property, and against MaxMin RLHF, which targets fairness across distinct preference *subpopulations* rather than the reward model's own graded distribution within one population

methods.name: GFPO
methods.shipped_by: no library implements GFPO as of this check. `huggingface/trl`'s top-level package export list (`trl/__init__.py`, main branch) exposes `GRPOTrainer` but no GFPO-named trainer; `volcengine/verl`'s advantage-estimator code (`verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py`, main branch) has no GFPO or metric-based-rejection advantage estimator, only an unrelated importance-sampling "rejection mask" for off-policy correction
methods.variant_of: GRPO
methods.data_it_needs: prompts with a verifiable ground-truth answer (the paper's RL stage used 72k math problems, of which the model saw 6.4k over 100 training steps at batch size 64), plus the same reward function GRPO would need
methods.extra_models: no value network, same as GRPO. The objective as written in the paper carries a KL term with coefficient $\beta$ and an entropy bonus with coefficient $\gamma$; the paper's own training run used $\beta = 0.001$ and $\gamma = 0.001$, so it did load a frozen reference model for the KL term
methods.when_to_pick: pick GFPO when you already run GRPO-style RLVR training, have a verifiable/scalar reward, and see GRPO inflating response length without a matching accuracy gain, and you can afford sampling more responses per prompt than you train on

methods.name: INSCL
methods.shipped_by: no post-training library in this survey packages InsCL as an importable trainer
methods.variant_of: Continual-T0 / random replay for continual instruction tuning
methods.data_it_needs: a stream of instruction-tuning tasks, each example an {instruction, input, output} triple (Table 1 of the paper shows this template); the paper's own scale is 765 English SuperNI tasks regrouped into 16 categories, LLaMA-7B as the base model, 2 epochs per task at batch size 64
methods.extra_models: none held for training in the sense of a second trained network - GPT-4 is used offline, once per instruction, to produce intent tags for the InsInfo metric, needing no gradients
methods.when_to_pick: pick InsCL over plain random replay when you are continually instruction-tuning one LLM on a stream of tasks, can hold a replay buffer of raw examples from every previous task, and want the replay budget itself to track task drift instead of being split evenly; in the paper's own Table 2, averaged over all 16 stages, InsCL beat random replay by 1.0-2.5 Relative Gain points depending on training order (Reverse/Random/Curriculum) and brought the standard deviation of Relative Gain down to about 3-9 (×10⁻⁴), against Random Replay's own 5-19 (×10⁻⁴) across the three orders

methods.name: PUMA
methods.full_name: propose a Personalized User Memory-enhanced Alignment
methods.shipped_by: no general-purpose RL/alignment library ships PUMA as a named trainer - it is a task-specific pipeline (memory retrieval + heuristic-SFT + DPO), not a single reusable algorithm
methods.variant_of: DPO, specialized by prepending a memory-retrieval and heuristic-SFT pipeline that generates the preference data DPO consumes
methods.data_it_needs: an instruction-function training set (to fine-tune web function selection), per-user historical behavior records (purchased-product metadata and review text, stored in a memory bank), and, for the DPO stage, pairs of best/worst function-parameter candidates per instruction with the associated instruction+memory+function context; the benchmark used is PersonalWAB, built from 1,000 Amazon-Review users, 40,000+ web behaviors and 9,000+ synthetic instructions, split 80% historical / 10% train / 10% test by timestamp
methods.extra_models: one frozen reference model $\pi_{ref}$, the SFT checkpoint, required by the DPO loss itself
methods.when_to_pick: a task where an LLM agent must call structured web functions (search, recommend, generate a review) personalized to one user's purchase-and-review history, and where a small self-hosted model is preferred over prompting a frontier model with the full history in context

methods.name: VPO
methods.shipped_by: no framework implements it. trl's top-level package exports no VPO-named trainer class (`trl/__init__.py` at commit checked lists `DPOTrainer`, `GRPOTrainer`, and others, no VPO); verl's PPO trainer config exposes only `adv_estimator: gae` as the algorithm default with no VPO option in its config file
methods.variant_of: DPO
methods.data_it_needs: the same preference triplets as DPO - a prompt $x$ and a preferred/unpreferred pair $(y_+, y_-)$ - plus a choice of calibration distribution $\pi_{\text{cal}}$, which the method does not fix and the paper sets per-experiment: the empirical distribution of ground-truth answers for offline ARC-Challenge, and the empirical distribution of previously-rejected ("negative") answers collected by the policy for the online TL;DR buffer setting
methods.extra_models: only a frozen reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$, exactly as DPO needs - forward passes only, no gradients
methods.when_to_pick: pick VPO over plain DPO when reward over-optimization or exploration coverage is the concern and a single scalar knob ($\alpha$, with its sign set by setting) is an acceptable substitute for an explicit uncertainty estimate; the paper's own offline result is that pessimistic VPO resists the accuracy collapse DPO showed past 1000 steps on ARC-Challenge

methods.name: SAPO
methods.shipped_by: trl (`GRPOTrainer` with `loss_type="sapo"`), verl (`actor_rollout_ref.actor.policy_loss.loss_mode: sapo`, function `compute_policy_loss_sapo`)
methods.variant_of: GRPO
methods.data_it_needs: the same as GRPO - prompts from the target distribution, with G completions sampled fresh from the current policy each step and a scalar reward per completion (on-policy)
methods.extra_models: none required by the method's own definition - neither the reprinted GRPO objective nor the SAPO objective in the paper carries a KL term or reference-model dependency, so SAPO's formula needs no frozen reference model and no value network
methods.when_to_pick: online RL with a per-response scalar reward, in the same setting as GRPO, when training shows the instability from hard clipping that the paper targets - particularly high token-ratio variance in MoE policies - and a smooth, tunable trust region is wanted over a fixed clip band

methods.name: HIR
methods.shipped_by: no library implementation was found in the searches this card ran
methods.variant_of: HER, adapted from goal-conditioned robotic RL to language-model instruction following
methods.data_it_needs: a set of queries (no instruction needed at start - the paper initializes the instruction to a fixed placeholder like "Generate a correct answer to this problem" and lets the offline phase relabel it [1, Sec. 4.2, A.2]); a scripted or learned feedback function `R(p,q,o)` that scores an output as correct/incorrect (the paper's BigBench experiments use a binary final-answer checker [1, Sec. 4.2, A.2]); and an instruction-generation function `φ` that maps a query, output, and score to a new instruction (scripted in the paper's experiments as swapping between two fixed instruction strings [1, Sec
methods.extra_models: none
methods.when_to_pick: offline supervised fine-tuning when you can score generations for correctness (a scripted checker, not necessarily a trained reward model) and want to reuse failed generations instead of discarding them, without standing up a value network or reward model

methods.name: RRM
methods.shipped_by: no library implements RRM as a named trainer or off-the-shelf recipe as of this check - searches of trl's and verl's own documentation pages for "robust reward model" and "RRM" returned no matches, and a GitHub repository search for "RRM robust reward model" surfaces only one unofficial third-party reimplementation, not a maintained library entry
methods.variant_of: pairwise/Bradley-Terry reward-model training
methods.data_it_needs: a preference dataset of triplets (prompt, chosen response, rejected response); the paper's own run used the RLHFlow-curated mixture of eight sources (HH-RLHF-Helpful, SHP, HelpSteer, PKU-SafeRLHF, UltraFeedback, UltraInteract, Distilabel-Capybara, Distilabel-Orca) totaling roughly 700K pairs before augmentation
methods.extra_models: none beyond the single reward model being trained - RRM's own definition needs no separate value network or frozen reference model at the reward-training stage
methods.when_to_pick: pick RRM when you are training or curating a pairwise/Bradley-Terry reward model from a preference dataset and want to reduce its sensitivity to response-only artifacts (length, format, boilerplate) before that reward model is used for anything downstream - best-of-N sampling, DPO-pair construction, or PPO-style RL. It is a fix applied at reward-model training time, not at policy-training time: RRM's own related-work section contrasts itself with ODIN, which decomposes the reward into an additive quality term and a length term and enforces disentanglement between them during reward-model learning, and with length-controlled DPO, which leaves the reward model untouched and instead adds a length penalty directly into the RLHF objective as a post-hoc adjustment during policy optimization

methods.name: SPIRAL
methods.full_name: Self-Play on Zero-Sum Games Incentivizes Reasoning
methods.shipped_by: only the paper's own repository, spiral-rl/spiral, run via `bash run.sh`; it depends on the `oat-llm` package (PyPI, from sail-sg/oat) for the distributed actor-learner infrastructure, vLLM for rollout inference, and TextArena for the game environments
methods.variant_of: REINFORCE, adapted to a shared-policy two-player self-play setting with a per-(game, role) EMA baseline (RAE) in place of REINFORCE's usual single global or per-timestep baseline
methods.data_it_needs: no human-labeled data of any kind — text observations come from the game engine (TextArena environments TicTacToe, Kuhn Poker, Simple Negotiation), and the only label is a single scalar reward per finished trajectory, the game outcome mapped to $\{-1,0,1\}$. Training is on-policy: every batch of trajectories is generated fresh by the current shared policy playing itself, with no replay buffer described in the algorithm
methods.extra_models: none required by the method's own definition
methods.when_to_pick: online RL for building general reasoning when the only supervision available is the win/lose/draw outcome of a two-player zero-sum game the model can play against itself, and you want to avoid curating problems or engineering a reward function

methods.name: BOND
methods.shipped_by: no open-source RL library implements BOND. trl's `docs/source/_toctree.yml` toctree has no BOND entry anywhere in it; its supported "Trainers" heading lists only DPO, GRPO, KTO, Reward, and RLOO (SFT is also there but is not an RL trainer), while PPO, Nash-MD, XPO, GKD, and several others sit under a separate "Experimental" heading the file itself marks `isExpanded: false`. verl's algorithm-doc index likewise has no BOND page (its latest index lists PPO, GRPO, DAPO, GPG, SPPO, SPIN and others but no BOND)
methods.variant_of: distills Best-of-N sampling into policy weights; not a direct variant of PPO or REINFORCE, though its backward-KL term reduces to a REINFORCE-style policy gradient (Eq. 15)
methods.data_it_needs: a prompt set only (no preference pairs required directly) plus a reward model that scores full generations; the paper's Gemma experiments used a set of conversational prompts, a previously SFT'd reference policy, and a separately trained reward model, at batch size 128
methods.extra_models: a reward model (assumed given, not trained by BOND itself); a frozen-at-each-step anchor policy, initialized as a copy of the reference policy and then updated online — either every M steps (vanilla iterative BOND) or via an exponential moving average with mixing rate $\eta$ (J-BOND, Eq. 18); no value network
methods.when_to_pick: choose BOND/J-BOND when you have a reward model and want a policy that reproduces Best-of-N-quality single samples without N-times inference cost, and you can afford generating from two policies (trained policy plus a moving anchor) every step

methods.name: ReMA
methods.shipped_by: trl's and verl's documentation carry no "ReMA" entry point as of this card (verl's README lists "ReMax," a different method, not "ReMA"); OpenRLHF, which the paper's own single-turn code is built on top of, and VeRL, which its multi-turn code uses for its single centralized training-pipeline controller, were not checked here for a ReMA entry point, so this card cannot claim no library anywhere ships it - only that the two frameworks checked do not
methods.variant_of: single-agent RL for LLM reasoning (VRP-RL / MRP-RL), decomposed into a two-agent Markov game and optimized per-agent with PPO, GRPO, or REINFORCE++ as the underlying gradient estimator
methods.data_it_needs: prompts with a verifiable outcome (math problems with a ground-truth answer) or a preference/judge label (RewardBench-style instruction plus two candidate responses); no separate chosen/rejected pairs are required beyond what the reward function scores at rollout time
methods.extra_models: the method's own definition needs two trainable LLM copies (high-level and low-level agents), which may be separate parameter sets or one shared-parameter model distinguished by system prompt in the multi-turn variant
methods.when_to_pick: pick ReMA when a single-pass reasoning policy under RL (VRP-RL, using GRPO or REINFORCE++) shows the inefficient-exploration/early-convergence failure mode the paper describes, and the task can be scored with an outcome reward (a verifiable answer or a judge label) so both agents can be rewarded from the same rollout

methods.name: KTO
methods.shipped_by: trl (`KTOTrainer`, `KTOConfig`, both top-level package exports at commit `2396dfe` on the `main` branch, read 2026-08-09). verl's algorithm documentation index (checked 2026-08-09) lists no `kto.html` page; this card did not check verl's source code or issue tracker beyond that index, so it claims only that KTO is absent from the algorithm doc index, not that verl has no other reference to KTO anywhere
methods.variant_of: DPO, sharing its RLHF reward reparameterization but replacing the paired Bradley-Terry preference model with a Kahneman-Tversky utility model over unpaired binary labels
methods.data_it_needs: one prompt-completion pair per example plus a boolean desirability label - no completion pairs required; trl's dataset schema is `{"prompt":..., "completion":..., "label": True/False}`
methods.extra_models: one frozen reference model, forward passes only, used both in the desirability term and to estimate a KL term from mismatched prompt-completion pairs in the batch - no value network and no reward model beyond the labels themselves
methods.when_to_pick: pick KTO when feedback arrives as a per-output binary label (thumbs-up/down, pass/fail) rather than as pairs, or when the desirable/undesirable classes are imbalanced - the paper calls this the natural choice for binary feedback

methods.name: SEAL
methods.shipped_by: no general post-training library (trl, verl, OpenRLHF core) implements SEAL. The only implementation found is the authors' own reference repository, hanshen95/SEAL, built on top of OpenRLHF, DeepSpeed and Transformers, exposing `examples/train_sft_selector.py` for data-selector training (Algorithms 1/2) and `examples/train_sft.py` for the fine-tuning stage, invoked via `deepspeed../train_sft_selector.py` from within `examples/scripts/` (which itself holds only shell wrapper scripts, e.g. `train_selector_llama3.sh`); it is installed from source with `pip install -e.`, not published as a PyPI package, and had 24 stars and a last push of 2025-02-20 as of this check
methods.variant_of: not a variant of PPO/DPO-style post-training methods; its algorithm is a direct application of the penalty-based bilevel gradient descent method to LLM data selection
methods.data_it_needs: two fixed, pre-collected datasets — a fine-tuning dataset D of N prompt-response pairs of mixed safety/quality, and a safe/alignment dataset D_safe of M prompt-response pairs with known-safe responses
methods.extra_models: none of value network, reference model, or reward model by SEAL's own definition; the training signal is each sample's own length-normalized negative log-likelihood loss
methods.when_to_pick: pick SEAL when you must fine-tune on a dataset of unknown or mixed safety quality, you have access to a separate, trusted safe/alignment dataset, and you can afford an extra bilevel training pass before the fine-tuning run itself

methods.name: APA
methods.shipped_by: no training-framework library implements APA. The paper's own code, heyjoonkim/APA on GitHub, is a script-driven research repository (`scripts/main.sh` calling `stage_0.sh`, `train.sh`, `stage_1.sh`), not a pip-installable package with an importable trainer class
methods.variant_of: supervised fine-tuning / instruction alignment, using the same family of curated-SFT motivation as LIMA, which APA's own related-work and results discussion cite for the "quality over quantity" argument it builds on
methods.data_it_needs: a QA dataset with explicit unambiguous/ambiguous labels and, for unambiguous items, a gold answer used to sort model predictions into correct/incorrect (paper uses AmbigQA for in-domain train/validation, with 5,287 unambiguous and 4,749 ambiguous training queries)
methods.extra_models: none
methods.when_to_pick: pick APA when you have a QA dataset with gold (un)ambiguous labels and gold answers/clarification targets, and you want a model that answers confidently on unambiguous queries but asks a clarifying question on ambiguous ones, without a reward model or preference pairs

methods.name: LOFIT
methods.shipped_by: no PEFT or RL-training library implements LoFiT. Checked by reading the top-level export lists of Hugging Face `peft` (`src/peft/__init__.py`) and `trl` (`trl/__init__.py`) at the `main` branch commit each resolved to on 2026-08-09 and finding no LoFiT-named export in either file
methods.variant_of: the learning-free localized representation-intervention framework instantiated by ITI and RepE, made two-step and learned
methods.data_it_needs: task examples with a gold label per example - cross-entropy fine-tuning on gold responses for CLUTRR and MQuAKE, or preference pairs (gold-truthful vs. untruthful response) for TruthfulQA, trained with DPO. No reward model and no scored-completion set is used; this is offline, small-sample supervised/preference fine-tuning, not on-policy sampling
methods.extra_models: none beyond the base model being tuned
methods.when_to_pick: a truthfulness- or reasoning-style task with a small labeled set (the paper uses 100-500 examples) where you want an auditable, tiny set of tuned attention heads rather than a dense weight update; pick LoRA instead when the task needs resurfacing memorized world knowledge, where the paper found LoFiT falls slightly short of LoRA and RED on commonsense/math benchmarks (SIQA, ARC-c, BoolQ, SVAMP); pick ITI or RepE instead only when no labeled training data is available at all, since both are learning-free and LoFiT requires a training phase

methods.name: URM
methods.shipped_by: no RL/alignment framework trainer implements URM. The authors released trained checkpoints on the Hugging Face Hub, `LxzGordon/URM-LLaMa-3.1-8B` and `LxzGordon/URM-LLaMa-3-8B`, loadable for inference with `AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True)`
methods.variant_of: multi-attribute reward models, e.g. the reward model in Nemotron-4 340B, with the deterministic value head replaced by a probabilistic one
methods.data_it_needs: for the attribute-regression stage, prompt-response pairs with multi-attribute human ratings; the paper trains on HelpSteer2 [1, App
methods.extra_models: none required to run URM itself beyond its own base LLM, which the paper initializes from an existing reward model - Liu and Zeng (2024) for the Llama3.1 URM and Dong et al. (2023a) for the Llama3 URM [1, Sec. 5.1] - identified in the released checkpoints' model cards as Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8B for URM(S) and FsfairX-LLaMA3-RM-v0.1 for URM(F) - before adding the probabilistic value head
methods.when_to_pick: pick URM when a reward model is trained offline on a static, attribute-annotated preference dataset and the downstream loop (best-of-n selection, iterative DPO, or PPO-style RLHF) can use a per-example uncertainty score to discard or penalize unreliable reward predictions

methods.name: SPT
methods.shipped_by: no packaged library implements SPT. The paper's own repository (`yellowtownhz/sycophancy-interpretability`, no license file declared in the repository metadata, 15 stars, not archived as of this reading) provides three script directories — `evaluation`, `path_patching`, and `pinpoint_tuning` — described as code for reproducing the paper, not a general-purpose trainer with a stable API. Building it on top of an existing framework requires two distinct pieces: (1) a circuit-diagnosis tool that runs path patching / activation patching over attention heads to rank them by causal effect on a target behavior (the paper's own `path_patching` scripts, or a general activation-patching library), and (2) a custom supervised trainer that sets `requires_grad=False` on every parameter except the Q/K/V/O (or Q/O for grouped-query-attention models) projections of the selected top-K heads — a loss on top of an existing SFT trainer, not a new sampling loop, but the selective-freezing logic is not exposed by off-the-shelf trainers (trl, peft) and would need to be written by hand
methods.variant_of: structured selective PEFT, per Ding et al.'s PEFT taxonomy, contrasted in the paper with full-parameter SFT as its main baseline and with reparameterized PEFT (LoRA) as an orthogonal alternative it can be combined with
methods.data_it_needs: multi-round question-answering transcripts built from existing QA datasets (the paper used subsets of MMLU, MATH, AQuA, and TriviaQA, sampled equally) reformatted into a challenge dialogue: the model answers, is told "I don't think that's right
methods.extra_models: none — SPT trains one model with a plain supervised loss (Algorithm 2), and the path-patching diagnosis step runs forward passes with activation interventions on that same pre-tuning checkpoint rather than a second trained model
methods.when_to_pick: pick SPT when a single, narrow behavior of an already-instruction-tuned chat model needs correcting (the paper's case is sycophancy) and you can build or reuse path-patching/circuit-analysis tooling to localize it first; the paper reports it matches or beats full SFT on the target metric while degrading general-task accuracy far less and shifting the output distribution far less (18x smaller KL on Llama-2-13B)

methods.name: SRPO
methods.full_name: we present two-Staged history-Resampling Policy Optimization
methods.shipped_by: no framework implements SRPO's two-stage curriculum or History Resampling as a named trainer or config
methods.variant_of: GRPO
methods.data_it_needs: prompts only, each paired with an automatic verifier rather than a preference label or a learned reward model score: math prompts checked by an equivalence verifier against a canonical answer, code prompts checked by executing generated code against up to ten test cases in a sandbox
methods.extra_models: none in the reported configuration
methods.when_to_pick: pick SRPO's recipe when running on-policy RLVR (rule-verifiable rewards, not learned preference labels) across more than one task domain from a single base model, and when vanilla GRPO on that mix is stalling because most sampled groups return identical, non-informative rewards

methods.name: MALT
methods.shipped_by: no framework this card checked implements MALT as a named trainer or recipe
methods.variant_of: DPO, applied per-role on top of an SFT stage the paper describes as analogous to STaR
methods.data_it_needs: a training set of `<question, ground-truth answer>` pairs only - the paper used GSM8K (7.47k train), MATH (7.5k train), and CSQA (9.74k train)
methods.extra_models: none beyond the three role copies of the same base model (Generator, Verifier, Refiner), which start identical and diverge only through per-role LoRA fine-tuning
methods.when_to_pick: pick MALT when a task has a checkable ground-truth answer (math, commonsense QA) and the goal is a specialized generate-verify-refine pipeline rather than a single model, and when synthetic role-specific preference data can be generated offline via search before any training happens

methods.name: JMLR
methods.full_name: Joint Medical LLM and Retrieval Training
methods.shipped_by: no packaged training library implements JMLR - it is not available as an importable trainer in trl or verl
methods.variant_of: RAG, with the retriever initialized from and structured as ColBERT
methods.data_it_needs: QA pairs, each with a gold answer choice and a rationale text, plus a background document corpus the retriever searches over
methods.extra_models: a retriever (ColBERT-initialized) is trained jointly with the LLM - this is the method's defining extra model, not optional
methods.when_to_pick: a domain QA task with a fixed document corpus, when you can afford to fine-tune both a retriever and an LLM together and want the retriever's document choices measured by whether they lower the LLM's loss, not by topical similarity alone

methods.name: CFT
methods.shipped_by: no library ships a distinct "CFT trainer." The method's own released code trains it as a standard supervised-fine-tuning run - the paper's GitHub repository instructs users to install LLaMA-Factory and run its training scripts over the critique-formatted WebInstruct-CFT data, and LLaMA-Factory's own supported-approaches table lists "Supervised Fine-Tuning" as one stage with no separate critique-tuning stage
methods.variant_of: SFT
methods.data_it_needs: (question, noisy response, critique) triples
methods.extra_models: a teacher/critique-generation model is required only at data-construction time, before training starts - the paper uses GPT-4o (and separately ablates GPT-4o-mini as a weaker teacher) to write the critiques
methods.when_to_pick: pick CFT when you have (or can synthesize) a set of question/noisy-response pairs and a strong critique-capable teacher model (the paper used GPT-4o), and you want reasoning gains from a single SFT-style pass rather than an RL loop

methods.name: ALORA
methods.full_name: an innovative approach we call allocating low-rank adaptation
methods.shipped_by: no library implements ALoRA. As of this check, HuggingFace PEFT's `PeftType` enum lists `ADALORA` and `GRALORA` but no `ALORA` entry (read from `src/peft/utils/peft_types.py` at HEAD of the `main` branch), and unauthenticated GitHub repository searches for "ALoRA allocating low-rank" (0 results) and "AB-LoRA" (69 results, of which the 30 sampled were all unrelated LoRaWAN-hardware repos) turned up no matching implementation repository
methods.variant_of: LoRA
methods.data_it_needs: the same supervised fine-tuning data as LoRA - input/target text pairs for the task, split into a training set and a small validation batch ($B_{val}$, batch size 32 in the paper) used only to compute the AB-LoRA importance scores
methods.extra_models: none beyond the base model being fine-tuned - no reward model, value network, or reference model
methods.when_to_pick: pick ALoRA over plain LoRA when the fixed per-module rank is suspected to be wasting budget on some Transformer weights while starving others, and you can afford periodic pruning-and-retraining rounds during fine-tuning; the paper reports comparable or lower peak training memory than SoRA (18.1GB vs. 18.8GB on LLaMA-2 7B / E2E) because it does not need to over-initialize ranks the way AdaLoRA, SoRA, and SaLoRA do

methods.name: ACT
methods.shipped_by: no mainstream RLHF/post-training library ships an ACT trainer as a top-level export - a directory listing of `trl/trainer` on trl's `main` branch (18 files, none named for ACT) and of `verl/trainer` on verl's `main` branch (13 entries, none named for ACT) found no ACT trainer in either
methods.variant_of: DPO
methods.data_it_needs: per turn, a prompt (task context plus dialogue history), a ground-truth response, and either a human-annotated or classifier-inferred dialogue action label from a fixed action space (the paper uses {CLARIFY, ANSWER})
methods.extra_models: beyond DPO's usual frozen reference policy $\pi_{ref}$ (initialized from the starting checkpoint), ACT's own definition requires three more models: a conditional generation model $M$ used only during preference-dataset construction to synthesize the initial losing response for the opposite action; an Action Classifier $A$, used during training to check the sampled response's implicit action (the paper's own implementation uses few-shot in-context learning, not a trained classifier); and a User Simulator $U$, used to simulate the next user turn when the sampled response continues a clarification trajectory (the paper's implementation is a second LLM prompted with a summarized user goal)
methods.when_to_pick: multi-turn dialogue tuning where the only usable reward signal is a discrete dialogue action (e.g., "should the agent ask a clarifying question or answer now") plus a task-specific correctness heuristic on the eventual outcome, and where labeled multi-turn preference data is scarce (the paper's settings use 50-250 conversations)

methods.name: DICE
methods.shipped_by: no library implementation was found in the sources read for this card - trl's DPOTrainer docs and verl's documentation index and algorithms overview page contain no mention of DICE, and the paper's own code release is a standalone research repo, not a library integration (github.com/sail-sg/dice, described by its own repository page as the official implementation of the paper)
methods.variant_of: DPO, used twice - once to produce the starting policy, once per bootstrapping round
methods.data_it_needs: a DPO-tuned starting policy plus the offline preference dataset used to train it (the paper draws ~10k pairs from UltraFeedback); no chosen/rejected labels are needed for the new data, since DICE manufactures its own pairs by ranking K=16 fresh samples per prompt with the implicit reward
methods.extra_models: a frozen reference model is required by definition, exactly as in ordinary DPO - the implicit reward is computed from the ratio of the trained policy to this reference; the paper sets the reference for round $t$ to the policy from round $t-2$ ($\pi_\theta^{(t-1)}$ is the target, $\pi_\theta^{(t-2)}$ the reference)
methods.when_to_pick: pick DICE when you already have a DPO-tuned checkpoint plus the offline preference data used to train it, want a second round of improvement, and want to avoid standing up any extra reward model or judge model

methods.name: LAB
methods.shipped_by: instructlab-training (`from instructlab.training import run_training, TrainingArgs, TorchrunArgs, DeepSpeedOptions`), PyPI package `instructlab-training`; its GitHub repository was not archived and had commits pushed as recently as 2026-07-31 as of this 2026-08-09 check. training-hub (`from training_hub import sft`), PyPI package `training-hub`, wraps the same instructlab-training backend behind a simplified call and is actively maintained by the Red Hat AI Innovation Team, last pushed 2026-08-06; its own support matrix lists SFT as "Implemented" via the InstructLab-Training backend
methods.variant_of: a taxonomy-guided variant of Self-Instruct-style synthetic data generation, combined with a two-step progressive training schedule the paper describes as similar to Orca 2's
methods.data_it_needs: a taxonomy whose leaf nodes each carry 1-3 manually written instruction-response example pairs, organized under three branches - knowledge (split first by document type, e.g. textbooks or manuals, then by domain, e.g. finance, each domain paired with source documents of permissible license for knowledge-SDG), foundational skills (seeded from four public sources cited by the paper: the FLAN collection [Longpre et al., 2023], MAmmoTH [Xiang Yue et al., 2023], a Stack Overflow question-answer mining dataset [Yin et al., 2018], and MuSiQue [Trivedi et al., 2022]), and compositional skills (tasks combining knowledge and foundational skills)
methods.extra_models: no value network, no reward model, and no frozen reference model at training time - LAB is SFT, not RL, so none of PPO/GRPO/DPO's auxiliary models apply
methods.when_to_pick: pick LAB when you need to instruction-tune a base model at scale from a defined taxonomy of tasks, without human annotators or a proprietary teacher, and you can supply 1-3 example pairs per task plus (for specialized domains) source documents

methods.name: BREAD
methods.full_name: Branched Rollouts from Expert Anchors Bridge SFT & RL
methods.shipped_by: no library implements BREAD as a named trainer at the time of this card - a GitHub code search for repositories matching "BREAD branched rollouts expert anchors" returned zero matching repositories as of 2026-08-09, and the paper does not state a code release
methods.variant_of: GRPO, itself a variant of PPO
methods.data_it_needs: prompts paired with a gold or expert-model-generated reasoning trace per question (the "expert solution" $S$ used both for correctness checking and as the EAS hint source)
methods.extra_models: no value network (inherited from GRPO)
methods.when_to_pick: pick BREAD over plain GRPO when training a small model on reasoning tasks where an expert/reference trace is available per question (human solution or larger-model rollout) and vanilla GRPO's rollout groups are frequently all-wrong, i.e., reward is sparse for the base model; the paper reports this regime for Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct on NuminaMath-CoT and MATH. Prefer plain SFT on the expert traces first only when the traces are short/simple enough for the student to imitate directly; the paper shows SFT on complex expert traces can decrease small-model accuracy (e.g., GPQA drops from 0.258 to 0.121 after SFT on S1K-1.1 for a 1.5B model), an effect it attributes to trace complexity exceeding SLM learning capacity

methods.name: PAL
methods.shipped_by: PAL's own README describes no trl or verl integration, and this card did not obtain a successful search of either library's own documentation or source for the term "PAL" (both GitHub code-search attempts returned an authentication error, not a result) — so whether trl or verl implements it is not checked, not confirmed absent
methods.variant_of: the Bradley-Terry-Luce reward-modeling approach used across RLHF alignment, reframed through Coombs' ideal point model
methods.data_it_needs: pairwise-comparison preference data where every example carries a user (or worker) identifier, in the reference implementation's own row format `(user_id, prompt, (response_1), (response_2)),y` with $y \in \{-1,+1\}$. No held-out chosen/rejected split beyond the pairwise label; no scalar per-answer reward is required at training time
methods.extra_models: none beyond the small learned mapping itself, in the framework's own definition — no value network, no separate frozen reference-policy KL term, and no LLM fine-tuning; PAL trains a lightweight learned function (a one-layer MLP in the synthetic experiments, a two-layer MLP with residual connection in the real-data experiments) on top of a frozen foundation-model embedding (Sentence-BERT `all-mpnet-base-v2` for text, CLIP-H/14 or PickScore embeddings for images)
methods.when_to_pick: pick PAL when your preference data carries a per-annotator or per-user identifier and you suspect preferences differ systematically across sub-populations rather than being noisy realizations of one shared reward — it is a reward-model training method, not a policy-training method, and its own reward model must be converted into a standard scalar reward model before use in a downstream RL pipeline such as PPO, per the maintainer's guidance in the repository's issue tracker

methods.name: UFT
methods.shipped_by: no library ships UFT as a named trainer
methods.variant_of: GRPO, extended with the hint mechanism introduced by R3
methods.data_it_needs: (question, solution, answer) triples where the solution is a real reasoning trace, not just a correctness label - the paper splits each solution into sentences and groups them into buckets to define hint granularity
methods.extra_models: the same as GRPO - a frozen reference policy for the KL term (coefficient $\beta$, paper default 0.001) - and no value network
methods.when_to_pick: online RL when full reference solutions (not just pass/fail labels) are available and you want one run that behaves like SFT while the model is weak and like RFT once it is strong, rather than a hard-cutover SFT-then-RL pipeline

methods.name: BLOB
methods.full_name: beyond post-training Bayesianization and propose Bayesian Low-Rank Adaptation by Backpropagation
methods.shipped_by: no PEFT-standard library (trl, peft) ships BLoB as of this reading
methods.variant_of: LoRA, with a Bayesian variational posterior added only on the $A$ matrix
methods.data_it_needs: the same data LoRA needs for supervised fine-tuning — labeled (prompt, correct-answer) pairs for the target task; the paper's in-distribution experiments use six common-sense reasoning datasets (Winogrande-small, Winogrande-medium, ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, OpenBookQA, BoolQ) with next-token logits over answer choices as the fine-tuning signal
methods.extra_models: none beyond the base model being fine-tuned

methods.name: RLSQM
methods.full_name: Reinforcement Learning from Static Quality Metrics
methods.shipped_by: no library implements RLSQM. A Hugging Face Hub model search for "RLSQM" returned zero results, checked 2026-08-10; a PyPI search for the same query could not be completed, since pypi.org returned a bot-detection challenge page instead of search results on every attempt, so PyPI is not usable as evidence either way
methods.variant_of: PPO, via the InstructGPT-style RLHF recipe
methods.data_it_needs: prompts built from a focal method plus adaptive focal-class context (entire focal file, shrunk in stages if it exceeds context length) and a filepath "hint" that primes the test's method signature - no target/label column, since the reward comes from a static analyzer, not from stored answers
methods.extra_models: three, all standard to the InstructGPT-style PPO recipe RLSQM copies: a value network (initialized from the reward model's weights, per Ouyang et al.); a reward model (a regression head trained to imitate the static analyzer's scalar score, Eq. 1); and an implicit reference policy - the paper's KL term is written against $\pi_{\theta_0}$, the policy's own initial (SFT) weights, not against a separately-loaded frozen copy the paper describes managing at inference time
methods.when_to_pick: pick RLSQM's recipe - PPO against a reward model trained on a deterministic, automatable checker - when the target quality signal can be computed by a static tool (syntax, structural properties, style rules) rather than requiring human judgment or program execution; the paper's own ablations show it clearly beats filtering-based SFT, its offline alternative, on the same base model and data (Fig. 4)

methods.name: TREEGRPO
methods.shipped_by: only the authors' own research repository, AMAP-ML/Tree-GRPO on GitHub (Apache-2.0, 393 stars as of this reading), which is a fork/extension of veRL and Search-R1, not a merge into either project's mainline
methods.variant_of: GRPO
methods.data_it_needs: prompts only (questions), no pre-collected chosen/rejected pairs or per-answer scores; the reward is a rule-based outcome score - Exact Match for single-/multi-hop QA, F1 for web-agent QA. On-policy: every rollout, including tree expansions, is generated fresh from the current policy $\pi_\theta$ each training step
methods.extra_models: no value network, inherited from GRPO. The objective's KL term needs a reference model $\pi_{ref}$, but per the paper's Algorithm 1 this reference is reset to the current policy $\pi_\theta$ at the start of every training step, not held fixed at an SFT checkpoint
methods.when_to_pick: multi-turn LLM agent RL with tool calls (e.g., search) under a limited token/tool-call rollout budget, where the only reward available is a single outcome score per trajectory

methods.name: GKD
methods.shipped_by: trl. Two different top-level entry points cover different parts of GKD's design space: `trl.experimental.gkd.GKDTrainer` (import from the `experimental` subpackage) implements the full paper — arbitrary student-data fraction $\lambda \in [0,1]$ mixing on-policy and fixed-dataset batches [5]; `trl.DistillationTrainer`, exported from TRL's top-level package (not experimental), implements only the fully on-policy special case ($\lambda=1$ fixed) with a memory-efficient chunked JSD loss and optional vLLM-accelerated generation, and documents itself as citing and implementing this paper [3]. A closed TRL pull request states that `GKDTrainer` now warns at init time when its config ($\lambda=1$, temperature$=1$) is exactly reproducible by `DistillationTrainer`, pointing users toward the latter for that case [6]. No other framework in this corpus's shortlist implements GKD.
methods.variant_of: Supervised KD [2] (which is itself built on classic KD [2]); GKD's on-policy limit ($\lambda=1$) is also what TRL ships as `DistillationTrainer` [3].
methods.data_it_needs: input prompts, optionally paired with fixed target sequences (ground-truth or teacher-generated) when $\lambda<1$; no reward signal, no preference pairs. TRL's `GKDTrainer` expects each row as a list of chat `messages` with `role` (`system`, `assistant`, or `user`) and `content`, i.e. conversational SFT-style data [5]. It is on-policy when $\lambda>0$: a Bernoulli draw per batch decides whether the student generates fresh completions that step or the batch is taken from the fixed dataset, so at $\lambda=1$ every batch is freshly sampled from the current student and no completions are ever reused across the whole run [1]. The paper's task-specific experiments used out-of-the-box T5 fine-tuning datasets (XSum, WMT en-de, GSM8K); the task-agnostic instruction-tuning run used FLAN2021 with 5.36M examples over 62 tasks [1].
methods.extra_models: one frozen teacher model, forward passes only, needed at every training step to score the (student- or dataset-) sequences (a required part of the method's own definition, not a framework default) [1]. No value network, no separate reward model, and no reference model for a KL penalty distinct from the teacher (the teacher plays that role directly, via the divergence in the loss) [1]. Cost details in Cost.
methods.when_to_pick: pick GKD when you have a larger teacher model and want to compress it into a smaller student while correcting the exposure-bias gap that plain sequence-level or token-level imitation leaves behind, and you can afford to run the student's own decoder during training [1]. Its parent, Supervised KD [2], is the offline alternative: cheaper per step (no generation from the student), appropriate when a fixed teacher-generated or ground-truth corpus is good enough. SeqKD, training on teacher-generated sequences via ordinary supervised fine-tuning, is the paper's other offline baseline; the paper's own text calls SeqKD computationally inefficient for generating data from the teacher during training, and for that reason skips it in the task-agnostic experiment, so SeqKD is not cheaper than on-policy GKD's generation cost - it was also outperformed by on-policy GKD where the paper does run it [1]. The nearest online neighbor is RLHF/RLAIF: GKD's own paper shows the two are not exclusive — Equation 5 combines a scalar-reward RL objective with the on-policy distillation loss in one weighted sum, to fine-tune with RL while limiting the "alignment tax" via distillation from a teacher [1].

methods.name: MiniLLM
methods.shipped_by: trl, `trl.experimental.minillm.MiniLLMTrainer` with `trl.experimental.minillm.MiniLLMConfig` [4]. The module sits under `trl.experimental`, whose package docstring calls it an "unstable or incubating" submodule where any trainer "may change (or be removed) in any release without deprecation" [5] — treat it as unsupported/experimental, not a stable trainer. No other framework in this corpus ships it. The original authors' own implementation is a from-scratch DeepSpeed/Megatron-style codebase (custom fork of `transformers`) rather than a plugin to an existing trainer, released at `microsoft/LMOps/minillm` [6].
methods.variant_of: word-level (forward-KLD) knowledge distillation [1].
methods.data_it_needs: a conditional generation dataset $\mathcal{D}$ of prompts with ground-truth responses (the paper used instruction-response pairs, e.g. Dolly, with 3-epoch SFT initialization on the same data) [1], plus an optional plain-text corpus $\mathcal{D}_{\text{PT}}$ used only for an auxiliary language-modeling loss that preserves general-NLP-benchmark performance; the paper uses OpenWebText for $\mathcal{D}_{\text{PT}}$ when distilling the GPT-2 family and the RoBERTa training corpus for the other model families [1]. No preference pairs and no separate reward model are required; the reward signal is the teacher's own per-token log-probability on student-sampled tokens [1]. On-policy: each training step samples fresh responses from a mixture of the student and the teacher (see How it works), not from a static pre-collected set [1]. Training scale in the paper: minibatch size 64, 256 sampled sequences collected per outer step, 4 inner epochs of policy optimization per collected batch, 5000 total steps, max length 512 [1].
methods.extra_models: a frozen teacher model, held only for forward passes to score student-sampled tokens and to contribute to the teacher-mixed sampling distribution [1]; no value network and no separate reward model. trl's `MiniLLMTrainer` follows this: it takes a `teacher_model` argument loaded via `teacher_model_init_kwargs`, and it is built on the GRPO trainer infrastructure, so it also accepts an optional `reward_funcs` argument for combining the reverse-KL signal with extra scalar rewards [4]; details in Cost.
methods.when_to_pick: pick MiniLLM when you have a strong white-box teacher (its own logits are readable) and want a student that avoids the teacher's low-quality long-tail generations, at the cost of running an RL-style training loop with online sampling [1]. Prefer plain word-level KD [1] when a single forward/backward pass per batch (no generation loop) is acceptable and the student is close in capacity to the teacher. Prefer SeqKD [1] (train on decoded teacher outputs) when you cannot backprop through the teacher's logits or only have API access. Nearest online neighbor is GKD [2]: GKD generalizes the same self-generated-rollout idea to a mixed on/off-policy schedule and lets the practitioner choose a JSD interpolation between forward and reverse KLD per token, rather than committing to full-trajectory reverse KLD with MiniLLM's variance-reduction machinery [2].

methods.name: SeqKD
methods.shipped_by: trl, but only under the experimental namespace `trl.experimental.gkd.GKDTrainer` with `GKDConfig(seq_kd=True, lmbda=0.0)` [6]; `GKDConfig` and `GKDTrainer` are exported from `trl/experimental/gkd/__init__.py` (`main` branch, commit `c3e240a`), not from the top-level `trl` package (`trl/__init__.py` does not list either name, `main` branch, commit `ef0a079`) [8][9]. trl's docs state that "the trl.experimental namespace provides a minimal, clearly separated space for fast iteration on new ideas" and that "anything under trl.experimental may change or be removed in any release (including patch versions) without prior deprecation," adding "do not rely on these APIs for production workloads" [10]. trl's separate, non-experimental `DistillationTrainer` implements only the on-policy GKD variant (student self-generates) and has no `seq_kd`-equivalent teacher-generation mode [11]. verl's on-policy distillation documentation (its `algo/opd.html` page and its async on-policy distillation recipe) describes only students sampling their own rollouts and matching a teacher's next-token log-probabilities on those self-generated sequences, with no mention of a fixed beam-search-generated dataset or of Kim and Rush's method by name [14][15]; no framework was found shipping the paper's own offline pipeline (build a static beam-search dataset once, then run ordinary `SFTTrainer`-style training on it). Building that offline pipeline requires no new loss, only a teacher beam-search decoding script plus a standard supervised fine-tuning run.
methods.variant_of: knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) [2], specialized from word-level to sequence-level targets by the SeqKD paper itself [1].
methods.data_it_needs: parallel (source, target) sequence pairs to run the teacher's beam search over; the student's SeqKD loss trains only against the teacher-generated targets, with no gold labels required at student-training time (mixing in gold data is the separate Seq-Inter variant) [1]. Paper's own scale: WMT 2014 English-German with about 4M training sentence pairs and a 50k-word vocabulary, and IWSLT 2015 Thai-English with 90k training sentences and a 25k-word vocabulary [1]. As defined by the paper, SeqKD is offline: the teacher-generated dataset is built once via beam search before student training begins, and student training is standard supervised learning over that fixed dataset, not fresh sampling from a live policy each step [1]. This offline separation is not preserved by trl's implementation; see Extra models and Cost.
methods.extra_models: as defined by the paper, the teacher is needed only to build the distilled dataset (beam-search forward passes) and can be discarded before student training starts; no value network, reference model, or reward model is used, and the training loss is plain cross-entropy [1]. trl's `GKDTrainer` with `seq_kd=True` does not preserve that separation: it keeps the teacher model loaded for the full training run and calls it every step the seq_kd branch triggers, and its loss compares student and teacher logits with a Jensen-Shannon divergence rather than plain cross-entropy on hard targets [6][7]. Details in Cost.
methods.when_to_pick: pick SeqKD when a trained teacher is available and the goal is a lightweight, one-pass compression recipe: run the teacher's beam search once over the training source data, then fine-tune a smaller student with plain cross-entropy on the generated targets, with no reference model and no per-step teacher calls at student-training time [1]. Its parent, word-level KD (Hinton et al. [2]), matches token-level distributions directly and needs no beam-search dataset-generation pass, but the SeqKD paper's own comparison shows it transferring less improvement on this NMT setup (Word-KD +0.7 vs. Seq-KD +4.2 BLEU greedy, 2x500 English-German student) [1]. The nearest offline alternative is the same paper's Seq-Inter, which instead picks the beam-search candidate closest by BLEU to the gold reference, interpolating teacher-generated data with the true target instead of discarding it [1]. The nearest online neighbor is GKD [5]: it generates from the student itself (not the teacher) during training and gets per-token feedback from the teacher on those self-generated sequences, and, averaged across T5 student sizes, GKD's own experiments report relative gains over the initial student of 2.1x on summarization, 1.7x on machine translation, and 1.9x on arithmetic reasoning, versus the gains from baseline KD methods including SeqKD [5].

methods.name: Distilling Step-by-Step
methods.shipped_by: no major post-training library (trl, verl) implements this method as a named trainer; trl's `GKDTrainer` is a different, unrelated on-policy distillation method [6]. The paper's own reference implementation, `google-research/distilling-step-by-step` on GitHub, builds a custom `TaskPrefixTrainer` on top of Hugging Face `transformers`' `Seq2SeqTrainer`, run via `run.py --model_type task_prefix` [7]. Building it elsewhere means adding a second seq2seq loss term to an existing seq2seq trainer, not a new sampling loop, since the method is fully offline and supervised.
methods.variant_of: knowledge distillation [2], using chain-of-thought prompting [3] to generate the extra supervision.
methods.data_it_needs: an unlabeled or labeled input set plus, for each input, a teacher-generated rationale and label obtained once via few-shot CoT prompting (each prompt is an input/rationale/label triplet exemplar) [1]. The label can be human-annotated ground truth (finetuning case) or the teacher's own predicted label (distillation case) [1]. Offline: rationales and labels are extracted from the frozen teacher once before student training begins, not resampled during training [1]. The paper's runs used e-SNLI (549,367 train), ANLI-R1 (16,946), CQA (8,766) and SVAMP (720) labeled/unlabeled examples, with SVAMP additionally augmented by up to 2,305 unlabeled ASDiv examples [1].
methods.extra_models: no value network, no reference model, no reward model. A teacher LLM (540B PaLM, or 20B GPT-NeoX in an ablation) is required only once, offline, to generate rationales and labels via CoT prompting; it is not loaded during student training or at deployment [1]. The student itself is a single T5 model trained with two forward/backward passes per step (label target, rationale target) through the same weights, detailed in Cost.
methods.when_to_pick: pick it when you can call a large teacher LLM offline (via CoT prompting) to generate rationales for your training inputs, and you want a small, cheaply deployable model that needs less labeled or unlabeled data than plain finetuning or distillation to match or beat that teacher's few-shot performance [1]. Prefer plain knowledge distillation [2] if you only have teacher-predicted labels and no rationale-generation budget. Prefer PINTO Tuning, the paper's own baseline, if you can tolerate keeping the teacher LLM in the loop at inference and want to feed its rationale as an extra input rather than train it as a second output [1]. The nearest online neighbor is STaR, which iteratively generates rationales, keeps only the ones that yield a correct answer, fine-tunes on those, and repeats the loop rather than extracting rationales once offline [5].

methods.name: DistiLLM
methods.shipped_by: no training framework in this corpus ships a `DistiLLM` trainer — checked against trl's docs (generalized-JSD `GKDTrainer`, not skew-KLD [8]) and against verl's README, which mentions only generic "distillation," not DistiLLM by name [7]. The paper's own reference implementation is the research repository `jongwooko/distillm` (PyTorch, no license file in the repo as of the commit read). Its README originally pinned a specific HuggingFace Transformers commit "by following MiniLLM," but a later changelog entry in the same README states that local-transformers dependency was removed on 2024-08-12 so the code could work with recent LLMs — the pin is superseded, not currently binding [6]. Building it on top of an existing SFT trainer would mean adding a custom skew-KLD/skew-RKLD loss plus a validation-driven, buffer-backed sampling loop around generation — a new loss and a new sampling scheduler, not a drop-in loss swap.
methods.variant_of: KD with KLD (Hinton et al., 2015) [2], skewing the divergence via the skew-divergence construction of Lee (2001) [1] and replacing MiniLLM/GKD's continual on-policy sampling with a scheduled, buffered off-policy variant [1].
methods.data_it_needs: a (source, target) sequence-pair dataset, i.e., prompts and reference completions, drawn from a fixed training set D (the paper's instruction-following runs use 14K training / 500 validation examples from databricks-dolly-15k, plus a language-modeling loss on OpenWebText) [1], evaluated against a frozen teacher model p(y|x); no separate reward or preference labels are required. Training is neither purely on-policy nor purely offline: each step samples one u ~ Unif(0,1) and compares it against two thresholds, λ_R (generation) and ϕ (buffer-use); because λ_R ≤ ϕ, whenever a step generates a fresh student completion into the replay buffer it also draws its training mini-batch from that buffer, and on other steps it falls back to the fixed dataset (Algorithm 1) [1].
methods.extra_models: one frozen teacher model p(y|x), used both to score log-probabilities in the skew-KLD loss and (occasionally) to validate loss on held-out data for the adaptive scheduler [1]; no separate reward model or judge. No value network or critic is used (this is not an RL method). Cost details in Cost.
methods.when_to_pick: choose DistiLLM over plain forward-KLD KD (Hinton et al. [2]) when mode-averaging or a training/inference mismatch is limiting a distilled student and some extra generation cost is affordable; choose it over MiniLLM's policy-gradient on-policy approach [4] or GKD's continual on-policy generalized-JSD training [5] when that on-policy cost (up to 5.5x slower per the paper's own runtime comparison, Fig. 7 [1]) is not affordable, since DistiLLM's adaptive scheduler keeps the SGO-generation frequency small throughout training [1]. It is not a preference-optimization method: the paper states DistiLLM is designed for a supervised fine-tuning setup and leaves extension to human-preference optimization as future work [1].

methods.name: SKD
methods.shipped_by: no widely-used training library implements SKD's token-level accept/resample loop. The paper's own reference code is the only available implementation: `google-research/google-research/tree/master/speculative_kd`, Apache-2.0 licensed, which documents needing 8x A100 80GB GPUs for its 7B-teacher/2B-student setup, and separately requires a patched `transformers==4.44.2` install (replacing `candidate_generator.py` and `utils.py`) for its vLLM-based inference/evaluation environment [5]. Building it inside an existing framework is a new-sampling-loop job, not a loss-on-top-of-an-existing-trainer job: it needs a modified generation loop that checks each student token against the teacher's top-K set and truncates/resamples mid-block, the same class of change as assisted/speculative-decoding candidate generation, before any distillation loss can be computed [1][5]. trl ships the parent method as `experimental.gkd.GKDTrainer` (On-Policy KD / GKD, `lmbda=1.0`), but it is exposed under trl's `experimental` namespace, and does not perform SKD's teacher-side token verification or resampling [2][4].
methods.variant_of: On-Policy KD / GKD [2].
methods.data_it_needs: prompts only (`x`) for the on-policy branch that SKD trains on; no fixed `(x, y)` pairs are required, since the response is generated on the fly and the training divergence is computed against the teacher's own token probabilities [1]. The paper's runs used prompt sets from ~100 (extreme low-data ablation) up to 1K (translation, summarization, GSM8K) to 10K (task-agnostic math instruction-following) [1]. On-policy: fresh student samples are drawn from the current policy at every training step, with the teacher intervening live during that same generation pass [1].
methods.extra_models: a teacher model `Mt`, frozen, run live during every training step to supply top-K token sets and resampled tokens, plus token-level probabilities for both models over the finished sequence to compute the divergence loss [1]; no value network and no separate reward model. This is the same two-model footprint as its parent On-Policy KD, but the teacher does strictly more work per step (block verification and on-demand resampling) than in plain on-policy KD (see Cost) [1][2].
methods.when_to_pick: pick SKD when you can run the teacher live during training (it must score the student's proposed tokens every block) and you want the student to train on its own inference-time distribution without inheriting on-policy KD's out-of-distribution-sample problem [1]. Its parent, On-Policy KD / GKD, is cheaper per step (no teacher-side resampling or block discarding) but the SKD paper's own Table 1 shows On-Policy KD can score far below plain supervised fine-tuning when the student is weak (e.g., 36.1 vs. 72.5 COMET on translation) [1][2]. The nearest offline alternative is Supervised KD, which trains on a fixed teacher-labeled dataset and needs no live teacher generation loop, at the cost of the same train/inference distribution mismatch the SKD paper targets [1]. The nearest online neighbor is ImitKD, which also blends teacher and student data but does so by randomly drawing whole sequences from the ground-truth set or the student's own output with fixed 50/50 probability, rather than SKD's per-token, teacher-adaptive replacement [1].

methods.name: Context Distillation
methods.shipped_by: no framework in this corpus implements context distillation under this name or definition. trl ships a `DistillationTrainer`, but it implements Generalized Knowledge Distillation - training a smaller, separately-initialized student on its own on-policy generations scored by a distinct teacher model via a chunked Jensen-Shannon-divergence loss - which is the classical-KD-with-on-policy-sampling case this card's "nearest online neighbor" contrast covers, not the same-weights, template-difference mechanism this paper defines [5]. verl ships a related but likewise separate-model trainer, On-Policy Distillation (OPD): its own documentation describes it as training a student model on states drawn from the student's own policy while using one or more separate teacher models as the source of the distillation signal, and its config requires a distinct teacher checkpoint per `distillation.teacher_models.<name>.model_path`, so - like trl's GKD - it is not the same-weights mechanism this paper defines [6]. Building context distillation would mean adding, on top of an existing generation and fine-tuning loop: a teacher-template / student-template pair, an answer extractor $f$, sampling of teacher completions from a frozen copy, and a token-level KL loss (approximated with an empirical distribution over a fixed number of samples per position, 100 in the paper) between the teacher's and student's next-token distributions - a new loss and data-generation pipeline layered on a standard trainer, not a new sampling loop from scratch [1].
methods.variant_of: knowledge distillation [2], specialized to a same-weights, prompt-difference-driven setting; the two narrower prior instances the paper subsumes are "context distillation" [3] and "prompt injection" [4].
methods.data_it_needs: a raw task input distribution $D$ of unlabeled strings for the target task - the paper draws these from an existing training split (e.g., a task's Natural-Instructions or SPIDER training examples) or synthesizes them by few-shot-prompting the same model [1]. No labels, preference pairs, or scalar rewards are required; the "label" is whatever the teacher template + frozen weights produce, filtered by the answer extractor $f$ [1]. Training scale in the paper's main runs: 4096 distillation examples for 1 epoch, batch size 16, AdamW, no weight decay, except the step-by-step-reasoning transfer experiment (10k distillation examples mixed with 65536 Natural-Instructions examples, 3 epochs) [1]. The method is not on-policy RL: within one context-distillation operation the teacher's parameters $\theta_{TEACHER}$ stay fixed throughout, though the teacher completions used for training are sampled fresh from that fixed model rather than drawn from a static, pre-collected dataset [1].
methods.extra_models: one frozen copy of the same weights, used only to sample teacher completions ($\theta_{TEACHER}$, fixed for the duration of one round) [1]; no value network, no separate reward model, and no judge model are part of the method's definition [1]. The only "reward" is the teacher's own generation, so the extra footprint is a second full copy of the model being trained, not a differently-sized model. Sequential distillation reuses the just-updated student as the next round's starting point, and the paper notes a further "recursive" variant, credited to Choi et al., in which the student itself becomes the new teacher next round, avoiding a separate frozen copy altogether [1]. See Cost for the memory implication of holding two copies during a round.
methods.when_to_pick: pick context distillation when you already have a prompt (instructions, explanations, in-context examples, or a scratch-pad) that measurably helps the same model, want to keep that gain without paying its extra inference-time tokens, and can synthesize or sample enough unlabeled task inputs to distill on [1]. Prefer plain supervised fine-tuning on the extracted answers (the paper's "directly learning with gradient descent" baseline) only if compute is tight enough that generating and KL-matching against 100 token samples per example is not affordable; the paper's own comparison shows gradient descent on the same examples underperforming context distillation by 8.6-9.0 exact-set-match points on SPIDER [1]. Prefer classical (cross-model) knowledge distillation [2] when the goal is compressing a large teacher into a smaller, differently-sized student rather than removing a prompt from a fixed-size model. The nearest online neighbor is Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD): GKD also trains a student on its own on-policy generations scored by a teacher, but the teacher there is a separate, typically larger model, not the same weights under a different prompt [5].
